# Open Stacks — Complete Text

> A research wiki on exploring the world's literature cheaply and well: what is free and legal (open-access books and papers, public domain), cheap and institutional access routes (subscriptions, public and university libraries), discovery and AI research tools, reading environments from e-ink to VR, the legal constraints on building tools, a reference architecture for a personal catalog of everything, and a gallery of interface mockups and prototypes. Maintained by QURI (quantifieduncertainty.org) as part of the CAIRN project. Every page is a dated working draft; prices and product statuses are as of October 2026.
>
> This is the entire wiki concatenated into one document, in book reading order,
> for offline reading (e-readers) and LLM context. Web version: https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org



================================================================================
# Start Here
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 2. What to Do First
Source: https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/decision-guide/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. This chapter condenses the chapters it links; every price, count and coverage figure comes from them and carries their dates (most checked 2026-10-15). An editorial pass on 2026-10-15 re-checked about fifteen load-bearing figures against their primary sources, among them SFPL's eligibility rule, O'Reilly's prices and AI clause, JSTOR's public-library policy, JPASS, Walters (2025), the Quest 3S price, Lau & Golder, DeepTRACE, Rao et al., the *Lancet* fabricated-reference rates, Undermind's benchmark, Claude Pro, the UC Berkeley Extension card, Link+ and the HTRC shutdown. Book-coverage figures come from small, hand-picked spot-checks (55 canonical books; 33 technical and 20 humanities books), and paper figures from one study of 875 cited works in seven fields, none of them ML, statistics or philosophy. Read them as rough, and as upper estimates for less famous lists. Unverified, and flagged where they come up: whether SFPL's JSTOR link works from home, whether O'Reilly's library edition carries the full catalog, whether a "Start Anytime" UC Berkeley Extension course qualifies for the \$25 library card, and every build-hour estimate. Sources: the linked chapters, which cite the primary sources, and the [research dossiers](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/tree/main/apps/open-stacks/research).*

This page puts in order what a Bay Area researcher should do to browse and read across thousands of books, textbooks and papers, cheaply and legally. Each step gives its time, its cash cost as of October 2026, what the evidence says it buys, and the chapter that holds the evidence. The order follows one rule from [The Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/): use up the free routes before spending anything, then spend on what is still missing, not on the whole list.

## The short version

- **Use the free routes first, and stop when your list is covered.** In the spot-checks almost all coverage arrived before any money was spent, most of it from one free library card ([The Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/)).
- **Tonight (\$0, about an hour):** install Unpaywall, open free Open Library and JSTOR accounts, learn the free-book routine, and apply online for a San Francisco Public Library (SFPL) card.
- **This week (\$0, one visit):** collect the SFPL card with photo ID. With legal free copies, its O'Reilly and Libby access reached 28 of 33 well-known technical books (85%). An individual O'Reilly plan costs \$499 a year ([O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/pricing/), October 2026).
- **Papers:** the free legal tools found some version of 73% of 875 cited works (58% in the final version); adding one university library's subscriptions raised that to 88% (85%) ([Walters 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12260569/), recomputed in [Open Papers and Preprints](/access/open-papers/)). Batch the rest into free walk-in visits.
- **Textbooks:** check the author's own book page first. Of 55 canonical books, 24 (44%) had a free legal text, including 8 of 10 in ML ([Open-Access Books and Textbooks](/access/open-books/)).
- **Subscriptions:** with an SFPL card, buy none by default; buy the last few books used. The five technical titles that no free route or Bay Area card reached cost \$159 together on 2026-10-15 ([Cheap Subscriptions](/access/subscriptions/)).
- **Pages inside books you can't read:** chaining Internet Archive search-inside, HTRC Extracted Features and HathiTrust's page search found printed page locations for one topic in 43 books in about 15 minutes, for \$0 ([Searching Inside Books](/finding/searching-inside-books/)).
- **AI tools:** start with the free core; the recommended paid bundle costs about \$45 a month at academic prices. AI search is precise, not exhaustive, and cited sources often fail to support the claim, so check references ([AI Research Assistants](/finding/ai-research-assistants/)).
- **VR:** don't buy a headset to read better. If space, travel or distraction is your constraint, test a returnable \$349.99 Quest 3S for two weeks ([VR and Spatial Computing](/environments/vr-and-spatial-computing/)).
- **Building:** buy content and paper search; build routing for books and chapters, which no product found in this research does [~80%]. Start with a weekend build (about \$22 and 12–20 hours [estimate]). Keep shadow-library files and licensed full text out of it ([Costs and Effort](/building/costs-and-effort/), [The Legal Map](/building/legal-map/)).

## The plan at a glance

Steps are in priority order. Costs are as of October 2026; coverage figures come from the samples in each linked chapter.

| # | Step | When | Time | Cost (Oct 2026) | What it buys (evidence) | Main catch | Details |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unpaywall extension; Google Scholar "All versions" | Tonight | 10 min; under a minute per paper | \$0 | Some free copy of 69% of cited works; the final version of 51% | Free routes reach only 36% of pre-2001 work and 3% of cited books | [Open Papers](/access/open-papers/) |
| 2 | Open Library and JSTOR accounts; the free-book routine | Tonight | 30 min; about a minute per title [inference] | \$0 | 24 of 55 canonical books (44%) free; 30 (55%) with lending. 10 JSTOR articles every 30 days | Terms range from CC BY to "on-screen only"; check the borrowable edition's language | [Open Books](/access/open-books/) |
| 3 | SFPL card; then an evening to add it to Libby, activate O'Reilly, test JSTOR and place holds | This week | One branch visit, plus 45 min | \$0 for Californians | With free copies: 28 of 33 technical titles (85%); 10 of 20 humanities titles | O'Reilly bans AI input; bestseller holds take weeks | [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/) |
| 4 | More cards: Peninsula–South Bay loop; East Bay; LAPL on a Los Angeles trip | Optional | An afternoon each | \$0 for Californians | Humanities ebooks in Libby: 10 → 16 of 20 (19 with LAPL). Technical: +1 title (CLRS, via LAPL) | Proof of address; LAPL is not worth a dedicated trip | [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/) |
| 5 | Walk-in sessions for paywalled papers | When the backlog justifies it | Half a day per visit [inference] | \$0 | A university library raised coverage from 73% to 88% (final versions 58% to 85%) | On site only; no systematic downloading | [University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/) |
| 6 | Buy the residue used | Per project | Days | \$8–\$70 per title | The last 10–15% of a list | Shipping time | [The Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/) |
| 7 | One month of one subscription | Only if a project needs it | Minutes | \$15–\$59 | Perlego: +2 humanities titles beyond six free cards | Personal use only; AI use banned or unverified | [Cheap Subscriptions](/access/subscriptions/) |
| 8 | Search inside books | Per topic | About 15 min | \$0 | Printed page locations for 43 of 52 HathiTrust-matched books in one test | Only 4 of 31 candidates from 2010 on could be borrowed or page-searched | [Searching Inside Books](/finding/searching-inside-books/) |
| 9 | AI research stack | This month | An evening [inference] | Free; paid bundle \$45–\$89/month | Precise search, citation graphs, feeds | Recall roughly 30–85% [estimate]; unsupported citations | [AI Research Assistants](/finding/ai-research-assistants/) |
| 10 | Two-week VR test | Optional | Two daily sessions for 10 working days | Up to about \$375, mostly refundable | Your own answer | Buy inside a return window | [VR and Spatial Computing](/environments/vr-and-spatial-computing/) |
| 11 | Weekend build with Claude Code | When you want a tool | 12–20 h [estimate] | About \$22 | A searchable, mapped shelf of about 10,000 free works | Hours are most of the cost | [Costs and Effort](/building/costs-and-effort/) |

## Two decision charts

The first chart routes one work to its cheapest legal copy, compressing the paper workflow in [Open Papers and Preprints](/access/open-papers/) and the book routine in [Open-Access Books and Textbooks](/access/open-books/).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  W["A work you want to read"] --> K{"Paper or book?"}
  K -->|Paper| P1["Unpaywall tab or OpenAlex DOI lookup"]
  P1 -->|no copy| P2["Google Scholar: All versions"]
  P2 -->|no copy| P3["Field server: arXiv, SSRN or RePEc, Europe PMC, PhilArchive, OSF"]
  P3 -->|no copy| P4["Author homepage; JSTOR free account for older or humanities work"]
  P4 -->|no copy| P5{"Needed this week?"}
  P5 -->|no| P6["Add to the next walk-in visit list, or email the author"]
  P5 -->|yes| P7["JPASS, a Springer+ month, or pay per view"]
  K -->|Book| B1{"Published 1930 or earlier?"}
  B1 -->|yes| B2["Gutenberg or HathiTrust full view"]
  B1 -->|no| B3["Author or publisher page, then DOAB"]
  B3 -->|not free| B4["Open Library: borrow the English edition"]
  B4 -->|not lendable| B5["SFPL: O'Reilly and Libby"]
  B5 -->|not held| B6["Other cards in Libby; Link+ for print"]
  B6 -->|not held| B7{"Only a chapter or a few pages?"}
  B7 -->|yes| B8["Search inside, then request those pages from a library"]
  B7 -->|no| B9{"Humanities monograph?"}
  B9 -->|yes| B10["One Perlego month"]
  B9 -->|no| B11["Buy used; an older edition is often far cheaper"]
  B10 -->|not there| B11
```

The second covers spending money or hours.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S["Tempted to spend money or hours"] --> Q{"On what?"}
  Q -->|Content| C1{"Did the free routine and an SFPL card miss it?"}
  C1 -->|no| C2["Spend nothing"]
  C1 -->|yes| C3{"Several titles from one service in one project?"}
  C3 -->|no| C4["Buy those titles used, or pay per item"]
  C3 -->|yes| C5["One month of that subscription, then cancel"]
  Q -->|Discovery tools| D1{"Mostly papers?"}
  D1 -->|yes| D2["Free core first; add Claude Pro, Undermind Pro and Scite Basic when you hit limits"]
  D1 -->|Books and chapters| D3["Little to buy: build the weekend tier"]
  Q -->|A headset| H1{"Is space, travel or distraction your constraint?"}
  H1 -->|no| H2["Don't buy one for reading"]
  H1 -->|yes| H3["Two-week returnable test, judged on week two"]
  Q -->|A tool| T1{"Used a weekend build for a few weeks?"}
  T1 -->|no| T2["Build the weekend tier first"]
  T1 -->|yes| T3["Month tier, if your reading is books scattered across sources"]
```

## Step 1. Tonight: the free routine

This costs \$0 and about an hour. Legal free copies alone covered a third of a famous technical list (11 of 33). In the 30-book probability, ML, forecasting and philosophy list worked through in [The Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/), open copies, the public domain and Open Library lending together covered 18 (60%).

**Papers.** Install the [Unpaywall](https://unpaywall.org/) browser extension, which shows a tab on an article page when a legal free copy exists. When it finds nothing, search the title in Google Scholar and open "All versions", which groups preprints, accepted manuscripts and repository copies. Together these found some version of 69% of Walters' 875 cited works, and the final version of 51%.

**Books.** The routine from [Open-Access Books and Textbooks](/access/open-books/):

1. **Published in 1930 or earlier?** It is in the US public domain ([Duke CSPD](https://cspd.law.duke.edu/publicdomainday/2026/)). Go to [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/) (79,598 ebooks on 2026-10-15) or HathiTrust full view. For a US book from 1931–1963, check HathiTrust too: US works from before 1964 needed a copyright renewal, so one that was never renewed may already be public domain.
2. **Otherwise, find the book's own website.** Search the title plus "pdf" or "book" and look for the author's or publisher's domain. This found 8 of the 10 canonical ML books.
3. **Read the terms** before saving or sharing. They run from CC BY to "personal use only" and "view the book on-screen".
4. **For scholarly monographs, search [DOAB](https://directory.doabooks.org/)** (92,260 books on 2026-10-15, mostly humanities and social science). Filter by publisher: 69% of its STEM books come from IntechOpen, MDPI and Frontiers, mostly edited collections.
5. **For in-copyright classics (1931–1989), use [Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/).** Open the specific edition and confirm the borrowable copy is in English: of the 12 test books Open Library flagged as borrowable, six were lendable only in translation or as a study guide.

**Accounts.** Open an Internet Archive / Open Library account: one-hour renewable loans in the browser, up to 10 books at a time ([Internet Archive](https://help.archive.org/help/borrowing-from-the-lending-library/)). Open a free [JSTOR account](https://about.jstor.org/oa-and-free/): 10 articles every 30 days, read online.

**Applications.** Submit SFPL's online form ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/welcome-new-cardholders)). If you will drive the loop in Step 2, also apply online to San José and the Peninsula Library System.

**Keep a list of the free copies you rely on,** with URL, edition, terms and last-checked date. Author-hosted books are the most valuable free layer for ML and statistics, the least indexed and the most fragile: on 2026-10-15 the host of *The Elements of Statistical Learning* was unreachable, and Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* is free in its first edition but sold only in its second ([sre.google](https://sre.google/books/)).

## Step 2. This week: library cards

**The SFPL card is the largest single gain on the ladder.** "Membership is free to all California residents": apply online, then "present a valid photo ID in-person at any SFPL location". No proof of address is asked ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/welcome-new-cardholders), checked 2026-10-15). The card unlocks ([SFPL databases](https://sfpl.org/articles-databases)):

- **O'Reilly for Public Libraries,** the platform behind the \$499-a-year individual plan. *Public Libraries* puts [~70%] on nearly all its books being readable through the library; nobody in this research logged in to check.
- **Libby,** LinkedIn Learning, ProQuest eBook Central, and EBSCO and Gale article databases.
- **A JSTOR link,** although JSTOR says public-library access "is limited to walk-in access".
- **Link+,** for print books held by other libraries.

In the technical spot-check, SFPL's O'Reilly held 14 of 33 titles and its Libby 10; with legal free copies they reached 28 (85%). The five missing were CLRS, AIMA, CS:APP, *Gödel, Escher, Bach* and Jaynes beyond chapter 3. Of 20 humanities titles the card reached 10, all through Libby.

**Which extra cards are worth an afternoon** (increments over SFPL, from the 2026-10-15 spot-checks in [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/)):

| You are… | Get | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| A technical reader on a laptop or Boox tablet | SFPL alone | All of the measured technical coverage |
| A technical reader on a Kindle or Kobo | SFPL plus San José | Libby editions of six titles that are otherwise only on O'Reilly or the free web. Neither device runs O'Reilly |
| A humanities or trade non-fiction reader | Santa Clara County first, then the Peninsula Library System and Berkeley | Humanities ebooks in Libby rise from 10 to 16 of 20 (Santa Clara County +4) |
| Not a California resident | Santa Clara County, in person | A free full card for anyone with a US mailing address ([SCCLD](https://sccld.org/card/)) |
| Passing through Los Angeles | LAPL | +1 technical title (CLRS) and +3 humanities titles. No O'Reilly |

**The afternoon.** The Peninsula–South Bay loop, by car: an SFPL branch (photo ID), a Peninsula Library System library (photo ID plus proof of address), a San José branch (photo ID plus proof of a California address), and a Santa Clara County branch (photo ID showing your current address). Every card is \$0. This loop supplied all eight extra technical Libby titles and five of the six extra humanities titles. The East Bay (Oakland, Berkeley) is a second afternoon, mainly for Berkeley's JSTOR link and in-library physics journals.

**The evening after (about 45 minutes).** Add every card to Libby, with hold notifications on. Activate O'Reilly from SFPL's database list. Test SFPL's JSTOR link from home: JSTOR says "Remote access for public libraries is not currently supported" ([JSTOR](https://about.jstor.org/products/fees/public-libraries/), checked 2026-10-15), but SFPL lists a remote link, and *Public Libraries* puts [~50%] on it working. The answer decides whether JPASS is ever worth buying. Finally, place holds at every library that has a book you want and take the first copy; with several queues, your wait is roughly the shortest one [inference].

**Holds are the real price.** On 2026-10-15, *Thinking, Fast and Slow* had 13 copies and 51 holds at SFPL, roughly 8–12 weeks for a new hold [inference]. A used *Superforecasting* cost \$9.38 that day. When the queue is longer than you will wait and the book is cheap, buy it.

**Print-only books:** use Link+ before interlibrary loan. It reaches "over 11 million items from 64 libraries", free, and "most LINK+ requests arrive in less than one week" ([Oakland PL](https://oaklandlibrary.org/borrow-from-another-library/), checked 2026-10-15). Only 5 of the 64 members are academic libraries, so expect it to be weaker for graduate texts [~70%].

**What the card does not license.** O'Reilly's membership agreement (updated 2024-10-09) forbids using content "as input or a prompt to a machine learning or AI system" without the copyright owner's written permission ([O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/membership-agreement/)). It does not mention libraries; *Public Libraries* puts [~75%] on it binding library patrons. Read in the library's apps, and give Claude your notes, the table of contents and the metadata.

**Get in-person cards while they are offered.** LAPL's instant e-card is now for Los Angeles City residents only, citing vendor licensing ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card/borrowing-policies-and-information)), and Orlando's library system stopped issuing fee cards on 2026-07-31. *Public Libraries* puts [~70%] on another widely recommended out-of-area route closing or narrowing by the end of 2027.

## Step 3. Getting any paper legally

Run the steps in order of time cost. "Measured" and "recomputed" figures come from Walters' 875 works cited in 2023 reviews in chemistry, materials science, cardiology, public health, economics, education and psychology ([Walters, *PNAS* 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12260569/)). The rest are estimates from [Open Papers and Preprints](/access/open-papers/).

| Step | Action | Time | Cumulative chance of a legal copy (any version / final) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unpaywall, or an OpenAlex DOI lookup | Seconds | 48% / 35% (measured) |
| 2 | Google Scholar, "All versions" | 1 min | 69% / 51% (recomputed) |
| 3 | ResearchGate and Academia.edu | 1–2 min | 72% / 57% (recomputed) |
| 4 | The field's server: arXiv; SSRN, RePEc; Europe PMC; PhilArchive; OSF | 2–3 min | 73% / 58% (recomputed); perhaps 74–76% with servers Walters did not test [~50%] |
| 5 | Author homepage, then CORE | 2–5 min | Perhaps 1–2 more points [~50%] |
| 6 | JSTOR free account | Minutes | Adds most for pre-2001 work, where steps 1–4 reach 36% [~60%] |
| 7 | A library: university login or walk-in; otherwise public-library databases and interlibrary loan | Same day to 2 weeks | 88% / 85% with a university library (recomputed); about 80% without [~50%] |
| 8 | Email the author | 1–14 days | About 85–92% without institutional access [~45%] |
| 9 | Pay: JPASS at \$1.66–\$1.95 a PDF, or the publisher's price | Minutes | About 95–100% |

**Field matters.** In ML, statistics, physics and mathematics, start at arXiv: posting there is the norm, so it usually ends the search [~80%]. Walters' fields leave these out, so expect higher coverage than his 73% [~70%]. In economics, expect a working paper: Scholar found some version of 72% of economics items but the final version of only 33%. For old work and books (36% of pre-2001 works and 1 of 37 cited books were legally free), go to a library first. When the free copy is a preprint, compare key tables with the published version before citing a number.

**Walk-in visits are the free library step.** UC Berkeley lets visitors use licensed databases on its public computers ([UCB](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visitors)). SF State's research stations need "no account or login" ([SF State accounts](https://library.sfsu.edu/accounts)), and you can save to your own USB drive ([SF State](https://library.sfsu.edu/community-borrowers)). Stanford gives anyone 7 free day passes a year ([Stanford](https://library.stanford.edu/about-stanford-libraries/visitor-access)). All as of October 2026. Run steps 1–6 at home first, bring a list of DOIs, and keep downloads to research scale: JSTOR forbids users to "systematically print out, download, reproduce or distribute" content ([JSTOR terms](https://about.jstor.org/terms/), 2026-04-24). Tag files you bring home "obtained on-site, personal use" so no later AI pipeline treats them as open.

**Asking the author.** No study measures how often a request for a copy succeeds. *Open Papers and Preprints* extrapolates from data-request studies: 50–70% within two weeks for papers under five years old with a working address, under 30% for papers over ten years old at the printed address [~55% that the true rates fall in these ranges]. Write to the current address and ask for the accepted manuscript.

**When to pay** (October 2026):

- **[JPASS](https://about.jstor.org/products/jpass/):** \$19.50 a month for 10 PDFs, or \$199 a year for 120. Only if you read a lot on JSTOR and SFPL's link fails from home.
- **[Springer+ Basic](https://link.springer.com/product/springer-plus):** \$39.99 for 10 chapters or articles in a month, against \$29.95–\$39.95 each pay-per-view. Queue the list, subscribe for a month, then cancel.
- **[DeepDyve](https://www.deepdyve.com/pricing):** \$499 a year for streamed papers. Against \$39.95 pay-per-view, it breaks even at about 12.5 otherwise unreachable articles a year.

**Remote university access costs more than its sticker price.** No paid community card at UC Berkeley, Stanford or SF State includes remote e-resources ([University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/)). UC Berkeley Extension students "enrolled in a semester-length (10+ week) course" can buy a six-month card for \$25 that includes remote access to licensed journals, databases and ebooks ([UC Berkeley Library](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/find/borrow-renew), checked 2026-10-15); the cheapest likely-qualifying course in an October 2026 sample was \$810, so about \$835 per six months. Whether a self-paced "Start Anytime" course counts is unverified [~60%]: ask the library's Privileges Desk first. A visiting-scholar appointment costs \$750 for the first year ([VSPA](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/about/university-services-fee)) but needs a faculty sponsor, and the norm is a PhD. Take Extension only if you want the course, the visiting-scholar route only with a real collaborator, and walk-in visits otherwise.

## Step 4. Free textbook copies

Where to look first, with hit rates from the 55-book test in [Open-Access Books and Textbooks](/access/open-books/):

| If you want | Look first at | Hit rate in the test | Then |
|---|---|---|---|
| A modern ML or AI textbook | The author's book page | 8 of 10 | The publisher's page; DOAB for MIT Press |
| A probability or statistics text | Author's page, then DOAB | 3 of 9, plus Jaynes ch. 1–3 | A free substitute; a library |
| Decision theory, forecasting, economics | Author's page, then DOAB | 2 of 9 | A free substitute; a library |
| An introduction to a new field | Open Textbook Library, OpenStax | Not tested | LibreTexts |
| A classic from 1930 or earlier | Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks | 6 of 6 | HathiTrust, Wikisource |
| An in-copyright classic, 1931–1989 | Open Library, English edition | 0 of 6 free; 4 of 6 borrowable | A library; buy used |
| Popular non-fiction since 1990 | Libby | 1 of 10 free | A hold, or buy used |

**Expect most of the famous ML books and little else.** Of the test's post-1990 technical textbooks, 17 of 33 (52%) are free, but only 9 of 23 (39%) outside ML. The list was chosen by an LLM, which probably favors famously free books [~75%]. Beyond that core, commercial textbook series barely appear in the open record: DOAB lists 3 *Graduate Texts in Mathematics* volumes. The free share of all modern textbooks is probably well under 20% [~75%].

**Free substitutes cover many gaps** (the chapter's judgments, not measured equivalences): [Grinstead & Snell](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf) or Durrett for Feller; [MIT OCW 6.041SC](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-041sc-probabilistic-systems-analysis-and-applied-probability-fall-2013/) for Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis; Erickson's [*Algorithms*](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/) (CC BY 4.0) for CLRS; Hernán & Robins's *What If* for Pearl's *Causality*.

**Open textbooks are introductory.** OpenStax (84 live titles; new and updated ones under CC BY-NC-SA since 2026-04-22, [OpenStax](https://openstax.org/blog/openstax-licensing)) and the [Open Textbook Library](https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks) (1,887 titles) suit a first course in an unfamiliar field, not graduate ML or statistics.

**Legal or pirated?** A legal free copy sits on the author's or publisher's site or in a recognised repository, and often says why it is free. A recent commercial textbook on an unrelated mirror or anonymous drive is very likely unauthorised. This wiki never routes to shadow libraries ([The Shadow Libraries](/access/shadow-libraries/)). And free to read is not free to reuse: 15 of the 24 free books are gratis copies with all rights reserved, which a personal tool may index locally but not redistribute.

## Step 5. Whether to buy a subscription

**The default is none.** With an SFPL card, O'Reilly Individual (\$499 a year) added no technical titles in the sample, if the library edition carries the same books [~70%]. Perlego's 5 technical hits were all reachable elsewhere. For humanities, a Perlego month lifted the six Bay Area cards from 16 to 18 of 20, at \$7.50–\$13.50 per added title ([The Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/)).

By what you mostly read (prices as of 2026-10-15, from [Cheap Subscriptions](/access/subscriptions/)):

| If you mainly read… | Buy | Cost (Oct 2026) | Why | Catch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Practitioner ML, data and systems books, and a library offers O'Reilly | **Nothing.** Get the card | \$0 | The same platform | Early releases and live events may be missing [inference] |
| Practitioner books, no library route | [O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/pricing/) a month (\$49) or three (\$129) at a time | \$49–\$499 | 14 of 33 technical titles, against Perlego's 5 | AI input banned; access ends when you stop paying |
| Theory texts (MIT Press, Cambridge, Springer, Pearson textbooks) | **No subscription.** Author PDFs, used copies, LAPL's Libby, a Springer+ month | Per title | O'Reilly had 0 and Perlego 1 of 11 such texts | Used AIMA (\$128) and CS:APP (\$93) are dear |
| Humanities, social-science or economics monographs | [Perlego](https://www.perlego.com/pricing/) Complete, \$79 for four months per project | \$79–\$199 | 8 of 20 against O'Reilly's 0; 153,000 Routledge titles | US rights vary by title; libraries had 16 of 20 famous titles anyway |
| Papers from the JSTOR backfile | The free account, then JPASS | \$0–\$199 a year | \$1.66 per PDF | 120-PDF cap; no bulk or AI use |
| Popular non-fiction | Library cards | \$0 | SFPL's Libby had 7 of 8 | Holds. Everand Plus (\$16.99 for 3 unlocks) only if holds limit you |

**If you can buy only one subscription, buy books instead.** The five technical titles SFPL's route missed cost \$159 at the cheapest AbeBooks listings, or \$315 if AIMA and CS:APP are bought used rather than as cheap "new" (probably international) copies: less than a year of O'Reilly, paid once, for books you keep. No single subscription covered more than 42% of either sample list. If you do pay for O'Reilly, buy quarters: eleven months as three quarters plus two months cost \$485, less than the annual plan.

**Skip for research reading:** Everand (unlocks cost \$5.66–\$11.99 per book), Kindle Unlimited (probably mostly self-published [~80%]; price unverified), a full year of Perlego, and DeepDyve without a heavy paywalled-paper load.

**Test your own list first.** Famous books favor libraries, and Perlego's strength is probably the long tail of monographs [~70%]. *Cheap Subscriptions* gives a one-hour protocol: list the 20–40 titles you expect to read, mark free copies, match O'Reilly's public sitemap, query Libby at each library, check Perlego, and compare each service's cost per added title with the used price.

**No subscription is a corpus.** Every plan is sold to individuals and cannot be pooled into a team tool; what each forbids an AI tool to do is in Step 9.

## Step 6. Searching inside books you don't have

For "which books discuss X, and on which pages?", a chain of free services answers without showing the text ([Searching Inside Books You Don't Have](/finding/searching-inside-books/), October 2026):

| Stage | Service | What it returns | Scriptable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary and eras | [Ngram Viewer](https://books.google.com/ngrams/info) | Yearly frequency of a phrase | Yes |
| Candidates | [Internet Archive / Open Library search-inside](https://openlibrary.org/search/inside) | Matching scanned books, up to 5 snippets each, counts by subject and year. Not the hit page: `page_num` is the scan's length | Yes, 1 request a second |
| Page location | [HTRC Extracted Features 2.5](https://htrc.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COM/pages/975306753/Extracted+Features+v.2.5) | Word counts per page for 18.7M volumes, 9.97M in copyright; CC BY 4.0 | Bulk files |
| Verification | [HathiTrust full-text search](https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/ls) | Page numbers and per-page counts, no text | No; by hand |
| Recent books | Google Books; Amazon Look Inside | A few snippets, previews, often the index | By hand |

**A worked run** asked which books discuss proper scoring rules. Search-inside returned 179 candidates. Of these, 52 matched a HathiTrust record, all search-only; printed pages were recovered for 43, and 17 had a section of three or more pages rather than a passing mention. The best hit was Lad (1996), pp. 334–357. It took about 15 minutes and \$0.

**Recency is the cliff.** Of candidates published before 1990, 82% could be borrowed or page-searched; of those since 2010, 4 of 31. For recent books, use previews and the back-of-book index, and expect to buy.

**Then route the hits:** borrow the lendable books in one sitting and read only the located pages; send one library request for older search-only chapters; check whether an edited-volume chapter reprints a free paper; spend money only on recent books whose previews confirm real treatment.

**Mirror the page data you need now.** HTRC's services closed on 2026-09-30 ([HTRC](https://analytics.hathitrust.org/)), and *Searching Inside Books* puts [~60%] on Extracted Features 2.5 still being downloadable from an official host on 2027-06-30. A 10,000-volume subset is about 2.4–3.9 GB.

## Step 7. AI research tools

**No product does the whole job;** a good personal stack uses about three tools ([AI Research Assistants](/finding/ai-research-assistants/), prices checked 2026-10-15):

| Job | Free default | Paid upgrade, if… | Cost (Oct 2026, billed annually) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Find papers | [Google Scholar Labs](https://scholar.googleblog.com/2026/06/scholar-labs-update-search-10x-faster.html); [Ai2 Asta](https://allenai.org/blog/asta) Paper Finder in exhaustive mode; Undermind's free tier | Undermind Pro, for more than a few hard searches a week | \$16/month academic, \$60 industry ([Undermind](https://www.undermind.ai/pricing)) |
| Synthesize | The research mode you already pay for, read as a map | Elicit Pro, only for weekly structured extraction | \$49/month ([Elicit](https://elicit.com/pricing)) |
| Is a claim contested? | Read the citing papers | Scite Basic | \$12/month ([Scite](https://scite.ai/pricing)) |
| Citation graphs | [Inciteful](https://inciteful.xyz/); Local Citation Network | Litmaps Pro or ResearchRabbit, for alerts | \$10/month |
| New-paper feeds | [Scholar Inbox](https://www.scholar-inbox.com/); Hugging Face Papers | None needed | Free |
| Library and reading | [Zotero 10](https://www.zotero.org/blog/zotero-10/); Scholar PDF Reader; Semantic Reader | Readwise Reader | \$9.99/month |

The core paid bundle, Claude Pro (\$17 a month annually; [Claude](https://claude.com/pricing)) plus Undermind Pro and Scite Basic, costs about \$45 a month at Undermind's academic price and \$89 at its industry price. Undermind and Scite can be called from Claude through MCP.

**What the evidence says.**

- **AI search is precise, not exhaustive.** Against four completed evidence syntheses, Elicit's search found on average 39.5% of the included studies, versus 94.5% for the librarian-built searches, at 5.5 times the precision ([Lau & Golder 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483133/)). Vendor figures of 93–97% mostly measure screening, a different task. The chapter's estimate for the best tools on exploratory queries is 30–85% recall [low to medium confidence]: fine for browsing a field, not enough to claim nobody has done X.
- **Cited sources usually exist but often don't support the claim.** Search-grounded systems invented 3–13% of cited URLs, and resolving every link cut that to under 1% ([Rao, Wong & Callison-Burch 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03173)). Deep-research modes left 12.5% (GPT-5) to 97.5% (Perplexity) of statements unsupported by any listed source ([DeepTRACE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04499), 2025 versions).
- **The literature now contains fabricated references:** 1 in 277 papers in early 2026, against 1 in 2,828 in 2023 ([STAT on the *Lancet* study](https://www.statnews.com/2026/05/07/lancet-study-finds-steep-rise-fraudulent-citations-academic-papers/)).
- **Books are nearly invisible** to these tools, which run on paper metadata. For books, use [Curation](/finding/curation/), [Browsing the Stacks](/finding/browsing-the-stacks/) and Step 6.

**Rules of use.** Resolve every reference and check five citations per report against the cited passage. Run any synthesis you will rely on twice and compare the cited sources. Before claiming a gap in the literature, search two different indexes and estimate what you missed with capture–recapture, N ≈ n₁n₂/m: if one search finds 30 relevant papers, the other 24, and 18 overlap, N ≈ 40, so your 36 miss about 4. Overlapping indexes miss the same papers, so treat N as a lower bound.

## Step 8. Whether to try VR

**Don't buy a headset to read better.** A 27-inch 4K or 5K monitor at 60 cm gives 67–90 pixels per degree (PPD); the Quest 3S gives about 20, the Vision Pro about 34, and Meta's announced VR Glasses promise 37. Headset text must be 3–4 times larger in visual angle, so only one or two pages are comfortably readable in view ([VR and Spatial Computing](/environments/vr-and-spatial-computing/)).

**The evidence is thin and mostly on old hardware.** In one study of 29 observers, reading took about 7% longer on a 13-PPD headset than on a ~60-PPD one, while legibility effects were about ten times larger. In the one controlled week of VR work ([Biener et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.03189)), 16 people on a Quest 2, compared with a physical setup at the same 1366×768 resolution, reported 35% higher task load, 48% more eye strain and 16% lower perceived productivity. Only 3 of 16 preferred VR. Against that, 4 of 10 self-selected long-term Vision Pro users work in it 5–8 hours a day ([Biener et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05067)): possible, not typical. No study compares comprehension on 2025–2026 headsets with a monitor.

**Who might gain:** readers short of space, reading while travelling, or fighting distraction, and anyone laying out many documents at once for a literature review.

**The cheapest experiment** (up to about \$375, mostly refundable):

1. **Free, one day:** enlarge your text to about 1° per em (about 30-point type at 60 cm) and work one page at a time. If that density is intolerable, a 20–35 PPD headset will be too.
2. **Hardware:** a Quest 3S (128 GB, \$349.99 since 2026-04-19; [Meta](https://www.meta.com/blog/update-meta-quest-pricing/)) from a seller whose return window covers two weeks. Stream your computer with Meta's free app, or Virtual Desktop (\$24.99).
3. **Design:** for 10 working days, read at least 60 minutes in the headset and 60 at your monitor each day, alternating which comes first, on the same kind of material. Log reading speed, a 5-question quiz, eye strain (1–7), and whether you would choose the headset tomorrow.
4. **Decide on days 6–10 only,** since adaptation dominated Biener's week. Keep it only if speed is at least 90% of the monitor's, quiz scores average no more than one question in five lower, eye strain no more than one point worse, and you would have chosen it on at least half the days. Otherwise return it.

The VR chapter's prior that you keep using it is [~20%], anchored on Biener's 3 of 16. For travel, run the same test with display glasses ([VITURE Luma](https://www.viture.com/), \$399). If text looked soft, the next tier is 33–37 PPD: Galaxy XR (\$1,799), Vision Pro (\$3,699), or Meta's VR Glasses (\$1,299.99, spring 2027).

**Cheaper device questions come first.** Paper beats screens on comprehension by a small margin (g = −0.21 across 54 studies), and e-readers did no better than tablets. Kobo e-readers borrow from Libby directly, Kindle gets Libby loans in the US only, and Boox is the only mainstream e-ink line that runs the O'Reilly app ([Reading Modes and Devices](/environments/reading-modes-and-devices/)).

## Step 9. Build or buy with Claude Code

**Services sell content (the right to read) and discovery (finding what to read).** A catalog you build is discovery only; content stays a separate decision, made in Steps 1–5. For papers, buy discovery: a \$144–\$588-a-year seat is cheaper than the hours to match it [~80%]. For books and chapters, build: R10 found no tool that places chapters from books, papers and lectures on one map and routes each to the best legal copy, and [Costs and Effort](/building/costs-and-effort/) knows of none [~80%].

**Your hours are most of the cost.** Hours are R10's unmeasured estimates for one strong developer driving Claude Code; there is about a 50% chance a first-time builder exceeds the upper end.

| Tier | Hours | Money (Oct 2026) | What it delivers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weekend | 12–20 | About \$22: Claude Pro \$20 plus \$1.50 of Haiku 5.5 batch summaries for 10,000 works; embeddings and hosting \$0 | A searchable shelf of about 10,000 free works, with summaries and a topic map |
| Month | 80–120 (100–140 with human checking) | \$510–\$1,360 in the worked example; \$165–\$425 with Haiku on the core shelf | A 100,000-work catalog with best-free-copy links and chapter-level search |
| Quarter | 300–450 | About \$650–\$18,100 | 10M works with incremental updates and quality dashboards |

At \$50–\$150 an hour, the month tier's hours are worth \$5,000–\$21,000. A year of four discovery subscriptions (Elicit, Undermind, Consensus, Claude Pro) costs \$1,124.

### What to build first

1. **A literature agent from parts** (an evening to a weekend [my estimate]). Claude Code with web search and [zotero-mcp](https://github.com/54yyyu/zotero-mcp), calling Undermind's MCP server (free plan), Asta's corpus tool and OpenAlex (a free key gives \$1 of calls a day) as tools. Put the rules from [AI Research Assistants](/finding/ai-research-assistants/) in your `CLAUDE.md`: no unresolved references, an evidence label on every claim, two indexes with the overlap reported. Call the engines; don't imitate them. On Undermind's own benchmark (vendor-run, 23 queries), Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code with web search found 47% of the top 20 relevant papers, against Undermind's 85%.
2. **Your access profile** (a few hours [my estimate]). Script the one-hour coverage test from [Cheap Subscriptions](/access/subscriptions/) over your reading list: free copies, O'Reilly's public sitemap (66,609 titles on 2026-10-15), Libby availability per library through OverDrive's undocumented catalog API, Open Library lending resolved to an English edition, and Unpaywall for DOIs. The output, your cheapest route for each title, is the seed of the resolver in [A Reference Architecture](/building/reference-architecture/). Query politely: scraping library catalogs is rated yellow.
3. **A mirror of the HTRC page data for your fields,** before the host goes (Step 6).
4. **The weekend tier:** a free shelf from Gutenberg, OpenStax and DOAB, with small-model summaries, client-side semantic search over a vector file under 50 MB, and free static hosting. *A Reference Architecture* gives a first instruction for Claude Code.
5. **The month tier only after using the weekend build for a few weeks [my suggestion],** and only if your reading is books and chapters scattered across sources.

### What not to build

| Don't | Why | Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild paper search or feeds | The engines lead (85% against 47% on Undermind's vendor-run benchmark), and a seat costs less than the hours | Call Undermind, Asta, Scite, Consensus and OpenAlex as tools |
| Feed licensed full text to a model | O'Reilly bans AI input; Elsevier (2026-03-12) bars use "in combination with an artificial intelligence tool" without a license; JSTOR bans LLM training | Metadata, tables of contents, your notes, openly licensed text |
| Automate downloads through a library or employer login | Rated red; publishers block whole IP ranges | The open copy, or a publisher's text-mining API under license |
| Let any shadow-library file in, even privately | Acquisition drove *Bartz v. Anthropic*'s \$1.5B settlement over 482,460 works, about \$3,000 per work ([settlement](https://www.anthropiccopyrightsettlement.com/)) | A resolver that says "no lawful copy found" |
| Store Google Books API results, scrape WorldCat, harvest YouTube transcripts | Red by contract | Live lookups, Open Library dumps, timestamped links |
| Break ebook DRM on a book you own | Red outside a narrow university exemption | Buy print or DRM-free; keep scans private |
| Run a server from day one | Static hosting should serve 100,000 works for \$0 a month (R10's design [~80%]) | Static until you need full-text chunk search or shared editing |
| Use frontier models for bulk jobs | Summaries of 100,000 books cost \$15 on Haiku 5.5, \$600 on Opus 5.5 (batch); thinking tokens bill as output | Small model for the long tail; a 1% pilot first |
| Build a virtual reading room first | No evidence yet that it helps reading | Step 8's test |

*The Legal Map* puts [~90%] on a personal tool carrying little legal risk if it avoids those red activities and keeps licensed PDFs away from cloud models unless the license allows it. A shared or public service changes most of the ratings.

## How much to trust this page

- **Coverage samples are small and favor famous books.** The standard error is about 6 points on 85% at n = 33 and 9 points on 80% at n = 20. The LLM-chosen 55-book list probably inflates the free share [~75%]. For a less famous list, read every coverage figure as an upper estimate [~70%].
- **Library results are one-day catalog lookups,** not logged-in tests.
- **The paper figures come from one study in seven fields;** coverage in arXiv-heavy fields should be higher [~70%].
- **The AI audits tested 2025 versions,** and rankings age fast.
- **The VR verdict rests on one controlled week** (n = 16, Quest 2) and a self-selected interview sample.
- **Build hours are unmeasured,** and prices are one-day snapshots that moved during 2026.

The disagreements that would change this plan are in [Cruxes](/start-here/cruxes/).

## If your situation differs

| If you… | Change the plan this way | Details |
|---|---|---|
| Live outside California | Santa Clara County gives anyone with a US mailing address a free full card in person; LAPL sells non-Californians a \$50 card in person. Don't rely on one remote fee card | [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/) |
| Have a university or employer login | Use it first for papers. Get the AI and text-mining clauses in writing before building on it | [University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/) |
| Read mostly ML and arXiv | Start papers at arXiv. The author-hosted canon covers most famous books; SFPL alone covered the technical sample | [Open Books](/access/open-books/) |
| Read mostly humanities, history or economics | The Peninsula–South Bay cards, Open Library for 1930–1989 classics, a JSTOR account, a Perlego month per project | [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/) |
| Read on a Kindle or Kobo | Libby reaches both (Kindle in the US only), O'Reilly neither. Add San José for Libby editions of O'Reilly titles | [Reading Modes and Devices](/environments/reading-modes-and-devices/) |
| Are an alumnus of another university | Check your alumni library and JSTOR alumni access before paying for anything | [University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/) |
| Want a tool to index books you buy | Buy print or DRM-free editions | [Your Own Library](/access/your-own-library/) |

## Open questions

- **Does SFPL's JSTOR link work from home?** Any cardholder can test it in five minutes; the estimate is [~50%]. It decides whether JPASS ever makes sense here.
- **Does O'Reilly for Public Libraries carry the full book catalog, and do its AI clauses bind library patrons?** Estimates [~70%] and [~75%]. Check a random sample of sitemap titles through a library login, and read the terms shown at first login.
- **Does a 3-unit "Start Anytime" Extension course qualify for the \$25 card?** Estimate [~60%]. Ask UC Berkeley Library's Privileges Desk, naming a course.
- **What does this plan cover on a list that isn't famous?** Draw about 300 titles at random from public syllabi in statistics, ML, economics and philosophy and run every step, reporting coverage by step with error bars.
- **What is legal paper coverage in ML, statistics and philosophy?** Rerun Walters' protocol on 100 works cited in recent reviews, with arXiv counted separately.
- **How often do authors answer a request for a copy,** by field and paper age? An opt-in logging tool could measure it.
- **Does a well-tooled Claude Code agent close the recall gap with Undermind** on forecasting, decision-theory and statistics queries, judged by people reading full text?
- **Does a headset at 35 PPD or more match a 4K monitor on comprehension** over 60–120-minute sessions? A Biener-style week on current hardware would settle it.
- **How many hours do real builds take?** Anyone building the weekend or month tier could log hours by phase and publish them.

# Part I — Getting the Text
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Open-Access Books and Textbooks
Source: https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/open-books/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. Counts, licences and link statuses are as of 2026-10-15 unless another date is given. The DOAB, OAPEN, Open Textbook Library and OpenStax figures are the research dossier's own counts from the official bulk exports and APIs on that date, recomputed in an independent verification pass. MIT Press Direct to Open figures come from Wikipedia because the press's own pages block automated access. In the 55-book coverage test, every "free" verdict except ESL's (host unreachable) was checked on a primary page, but most "not free" verdicts rest on the research agent's prior knowledge rather than a page-by-page search. Sources: the [R01 dossier](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/blob/main/apps/open-stacks/research/R01-open-books.md) and primary sources linked inline.*

This chapter covers books and textbooks that are free and legal to read: public domain, openly licensed, or posted in full by the author or publisher. Papers have [their own chapter](/access/open-papers/), as do [the public domain and large open corpora](/access/public-domain/), library lending ([Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/)) and [the shadow libraries](/access/shadow-libraries/).

## The short version

- **In a test of 55 frequently recommended books across six fields, 24 (44%) have a free, legal full text.** The list was chosen by an LLM, which probably biases it toward famously free titles. The split by field is lopsided: ML/AI 8 of 10, probability and statistics 3 of 9, decision theory and economics 2 of 9.
- **Era matters as much as field.** Post-1990 technical textbooks: 17 of 33 free (52%). Pre-1929 classics: 6 of 6. In-copyright classics from 1930–1989 (Feller, Savage, Kuhn, Popper, Parfit, Brooks): 0 of 6. Popular non-fiction since 1990: 1 of 10.
- **Controlled digital lending adds 11 points.** Counting books with a borrowable English scan on Open Library, 30 of 55 (55%) can be read free and legally. A higher figure, 36 of 55, counts six books whose only lendable copy is a translation or a study guide.
- **Free to read is not free to reuse.** Only 7 of the 55 are public domain or under CC BY / CC BY-SA. Fifteen of the 24 free books are gratis PDFs or HTML posted by authors or publishers with all rights reserved, often "personal use only".
- **The claim that free legal sources cover under 20% of modern technical textbooks is false for the canonical core and probably true for the long tail.** Mainstream commercial series are almost absent from the open record: DOAB lists 3 *Graduate Texts in Mathematics* volumes and 0 *Undergraduate Topics in Computer Science*.
- **The most valuable layer is the least indexed.** The free ML and statistics canon (Bishop, ESL, ISL, Murphy, MacKay, Sutton & Barto, BDA3, Boyd) lives on author and publisher pages, not in DOAB or any structured catalog. It is also the most fragile layer.
- **DOAB is large (about 92,000 books) but mostly humanities and social science, and 69% of its STEM books come from three publishers** of edited collections and journal special-issue reprints: IntechOpen, MDPI and Frontiers.
- **OpenStax moved new and updated titles to CC BY-NC-SA on 2026-04-22**, after a March post blaming AI-accelerated commercial reuse. Older CC BY versions stay reusable.
- **If you do one thing:** for a modern technical book, check the author's own book page before anything else. For anything published 1930–1989, go straight to [Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/) and check whether the *English* edition is borrowable.

## How much is free: a test on 55 books

### Method

The research agent that wrote the dossier, an LLM, picked 55 books often named in reading lists and syllabi, 9 or 10 in each of six fields. It deliberately mixed "famously free" and "famously paid" titles, and practitioner bestsellers with academic texts. For each book it searched the [DOAB](https://directory.doabooks.org/) export and the [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/) catalogue and recorded the [Open Library](https://openlibrary.org/dev/docs/api/search) lending status on 2026-10-15. It opened the author's or publisher's page for every book it rated free, but for only four it rated not free (see below).

"Free legal full text" means one of three things: public domain in the US, an open licence, or a complete text deliberately posted by the author or publisher. Partial texts and controlled digital lending (CDL) are counted separately.

### Limits of the sample

Read the numbers below as a rough map, not a measurement.

- **The list is LLM-chosen, and the choice is partly circular.** Free books are discussed, linked and recommended more often on the web, and a model's sense of "the canon" comes from web text. So a model-picked canon over-represents famously free books. The bias most likely pushes the free share *up* [~75%].
- **The sample is small.** At n=55 the binomial standard error on 44% is about 7 points, so a 95% interval runs roughly 31–57%. Each field has only 9 or 10 books, so a field's share could easily move 30 points with a different list.
- **Other lists would give other numbers.** The dossier judges that another analyst's list could plausibly put modern technical textbooks anywhere from 35% to 60% free. The share is most sensitive to how many ML books are included.
- **"Not free" is less certain than "free."** Of the 31 non-free verdicts (including Jaynes, which is partial), only AIMA, Wasserman, Kleppmann and Jaynes were checked on the author's or publisher's page; McElreath's site refused the check. The other 27 rely on prior knowledge [high confidence, not certainty]. An unnoticed free copy would raise the share.
- **Two free verdicts carry residual doubt.** Blitzstein & Hwang's free PDF sits on Google Drive behind the authors' domain, and the course site that would show the publisher's permission refused automated access [~80% authorised]. The host of *Elements of Statistical Learning* was unreachable in every check on 2026-10-15, but the Internet Archive [records a successful capture](https://archive.org/wayback/available?url=hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/) of the book page on 2026-10-04 [~90% that the long-standing free PDF is still served to browsers].

### Results by field

| Field | n | Free legal full text | Partial | Plus a borrowable English scan (CDL) | Free or borrowable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability & statistics | 9 | 3 (33%) | 1 (Jaynes, ch. 1–3) | +2 | 5 (56%) |
| ML / AI | 10 | **8 (80%)** | 0 | +1 | 9 (90%) |
| Decision theory, forecasting, economics | 9 | 2 (22%) | 0 | +1 | 3 (33%) |
| Philosophy, rationality | 9 | 4 (44%) | 0 | +2 | 6 (67%) |
| History, social science | 9 | 4 (44%, all pre-1900 public domain) | 0 | +0 | 4 (44%) |
| Software engineering | 9 | 3 (33%) | 0 | +0 | 3 (33%) |
| **Total** | **55** | **24 (44%)** | **1** | **+6** | **30 (55%)** |

Open Library's search API flags 12 of the 31 non-free books as "borrowable", but that flag is a maximum over every edition of a work, including translations. Checking each edition's Internet Archive item shows that six of the twelve (Kahneman, Mankiw, Diamond, Harari, Acemoglu & Robinson, Brooks) have no lendable English edition: the lendable copy is a Dutch, Korean, German, Polish, Spanish, Swedish or Chinese translation, or, for Mankiw, a 2001 study guide. For *Thinking, Fast and Slow*, for example, the [editions list](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL15992072W/editions.json) has three English scans, all print-disabled only, while the Dutch and Korean scans are lendable (checked 2026-10-15). Counting translations, the total reaches 36 of 55 (65%), or 37 with Popper, whose main work record is flagged through a Galician translation. For an English reader, 30 of 55 is the right figure.

### Which books

| Field | Free (type) | Not free, but an English scan is borrowable | Not free |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probability & statistics | Blitzstein & Hwang, *Introduction to Probability* 2e (gratis); Gelman et al., *Bayesian Data Analysis* 3e (gratis, non-commercial); Gelman, Hill & Vehtari, *Regression and Other Stories* (gratis, personal use). Partial: Jaynes, *Probability Theory* (ch. 1–3) | Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, *Introduction to Probability* 2e; Feller, Vol. 1 | Wasserman, *All of Statistics*; Casella & Berger; McElreath, *Statistical Rethinking* 2e (lectures free) |
| ML / AI | Bishop, *PRML*; Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *ESL*; James et al., *ISL*; Murphy, *Probabilistic ML* (CC BY-NC-ND); Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning* (HTML only); Sutton & Barto; MacKay, *ITILA*; Prince, *Understanding Deep Learning* | Géron, *Hands-On ML* (1st edition only; the sample entry was the 3rd) | Russell & Norvig, *AIMA* 4e |
| Decision theory, forecasting, economics | Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* 3e; Osborne & Rubinstein, *A Course in Game Theory* | Savage, *The Foundations of Statistics* | Tetlock & Gardner, *Superforecasting*; Kahneman, *Thinking, Fast and Slow*; Peterson, *An Introduction to Decision Theory*; Hubbard, *How to Measure Anything*; Mas-Colell, Whinston & Green; Mankiw, *Principles of Economics* |
| Philosophy, rationality | Yudkowsky, *Rationality: From AI to Zombies* (gratis); Hume, *Treatise* (PD); Mill, *Utilitarianism* (PD); MacAskill, Bykvist & Ord, *Moral Uncertainty* (CC BY-NC-ND) | Parfit, *Reasons and Persons*; Kuhn, *Structure of Scientific Revolutions* | Popper, *Logic of Scientific Discovery*; Pearl, *Causality* 2e; Bostrom, *Superintelligence* |
| History, social science | Gibbon; Thucydides (Crawley tr.); Smith, *Wealth of Nations*; Tocqueville (Reeve tr.) (all PD) | none | Diamond; Harari; Pinker, *Better Angels*; Acemoglu & Robinson; Scott, *Seeing Like a State* |
| Software engineering | Abelson & Sussman, *SICP* 2e (CC BY-SA 4.0); Arpaci-Dusseau, *OSTEP* (gratis); Beyer et al., *Site Reliability Engineering* (1st edition only) | none | Brooks, *Mythical Man-Month*; Kleppmann, *DDIA*; Martin, *Clean Code*; Thomas & Hunt, *Pragmatic Programmer*; Gamma et al., *Design Patterns*; Cormen et al., *CLRS* 4e |

### Results by era and genre

Era separates free from paid as sharply as field does.

| Segment | n | Free | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Post-1990 technical textbooks and monographs (statistics, ML, economics and decision theory, software engineering, causality) | 33 | 17 | **52%** |
| … the same, excluding ML/AI | 23 | 9 | 39% |
| Popular or general non-fiction since 1990 | 10 | 1 (*Rationality: From AI to Zombies*) | 10% |
| Pre-1929 classics | 6 | 6 | 100% |
| In-copyright classics, 1930–1989 | 6 | **0** | **0%** |

The 1930–1989 hole is the biggest gap. Four of those six (Feller, Savage, Kuhn, Parfit) have a borrowable English scan on Open Library; Popper and Brooks are lendable only in translation. The hole closes slowly. Works published before 1978 get a 95-year US term, so one publication year enters the public domain each January: 1930 works did on 2026-01-01, including Freud's *Civilization and Its Discontents* (in the original German) and Russell's *The Conquest of Happiness* ([Duke CSPD, Public Domain Day 2026](https://cspd.law.duke.edu/publicdomainday/2026/)). Books from 1978 on, such as *Reasons and Persons* (1984), run for the author's life plus 70 years. One shortcut: US works published before 1964 also needed a copyright renewal (same Duke page), so a mid-century US book whose renewal lapsed is already public domain; foreign works do not get this exemption. For a 1931–1963 US book, check HathiTrust for full view before borrowing; [The Public Domain and Open Corpora](/access/public-domain/) covers how.

### Free to read versus free to reuse

| Kind of free text | Count | Share of the 24 free | Books |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gratis: posted by author or publisher, all rights reserved | 15 | 62.5% | Blitzstein & Hwang, BDA3, ROS, PRML, ESL, ISL, Goodfellow, Sutton & Barto, MacKay, Prince, FPP3, Osborne & Rubinstein, *Rationality: A–Z*, OSTEP, SRE |
| Public domain | 6 | 25% | Hume, Mill, Gibbon, Thucydides, Smith, Tocqueville |
| Creative Commons | 3 | 12.5% | Murphy (BY-NC-ND), *Moral Uncertainty* (BY-NC-ND), SICP (BY-SA 4.0) |
| **Reusable commercially (PD, CC BY or CC BY-SA)** | **7 of 55** | **13% of the sample** | the six PD books plus SICP |

The gratis terms vary and matter. *Regression and Other Stories* is posted "for personal use only … With permission from Cambridge University Press" ([ROS page](https://avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples/)). BDA3 is "for non-commercial purposes" ([BDA page](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/)). MacKay's page says "You are welcome to view the book on-screen" ([ITILA](https://www.inference.org.uk/itila/book.html)). Goodfellow et al. offer HTML only, because "our contract with MIT Press forbids distribution of too easily copied electronic formats" ([deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/)).

For a reader this distinction rarely matters. For a tool it decides the architecture. Sort every document into one of three licence lanes:

- **Lane A (PD, CC BY, CC BY-SA):** you may redistribute, embed and use commercially. 13% of the sample.
- **Lane B (CC NC or ND):** you may share copies non-commercially; NC rules out commercial use and ND rules out adapted versions. Whether embeddings or summaries count as adaptations is unsettled, so keep lane B out of commercial products [I].
- **Lane C (gratis, personal use):** link out, index locally for your own use, never redistribute. Together, lanes A to C cover 44% of the sample.

[The Legal Map](/building/legal-map/) covers what each lane permits in more detail.

## Verdict on the under-20% claim

The claim under test: *free legal sources cover under 20% of the modern technical textbooks someone would want.*

**For the canonical core, it is false.** In the sample, 17 of 33 post-1990 technical books are free (52%; 95% interval roughly 35–69% from sample size alone), 9 of 23 without ML (39%), and 8 of 10 in ML. Even if the LLM-chosen list inflates the share by 15–20 points, the core stays above 20% [~80%].

**For the long tail, it is probably true.** Commercial textbook series barely appear in the open-access record. Counts from the DOAB export, 2026-10-15:

| Series | Volumes in DOAB | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Springer *Graduate Texts in Mathematics* | 3 | Axler, *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis*; *Metric Lie Groups*; *Quaternion Algebras* |
| Springer *Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics* | 2 | Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right* 4e; *Beginning in Algebraic Geometry* |
| *Springer Texts in Statistics* | 1 | |
| *Springer Series in Statistics* | 1 | |
| *Undergraduate Topics in Computer Science* | 0 | |
| *Texts in Computer Science* | 0 | |
| *Universitext* | 0 | |
| CRC *Texts in Statistical Science* | 0 | |
| MIT *Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning* | 4 | *Boosting*; *Gaussian Processes for ML*; *ML for Data Streams*; *Distributional RL* |

GTM alone runs to around 300 volumes [~70% on the exact figure], so the openly licensed share of the mainstream series is likely at most 2–5% [medium confidence]. DOAB undercounts, because author-hosted PDFs never enter it: ISL is itself a *Springer Texts in Statistics* volume, and ESL is in *Springer Series in Statistics*. Even allowing for that, the free share of the full universe of modern textbooks is probably well under 20% [~75%].

**What you want decides which answer applies.** Someone reading ML, Bayesian statistics and forecasting lives in an unusually open world: most of the books they will reach for first are free. Someone reading microeconomic theory, decision theory, algorithms or classic software engineering texts should expect a third or less, and should plan on a library or a purchase for the rest. I lean that the useful framing is "most of the famous ML books, little of everything else" [~75%].

| [OAPEN Library](https://library.oapen.org/) | Full-text repository behind much of DOAB | 36,434 books, 6,504 chapters | Per book | Same, more European, more HSS | 83% HSS among classified books |

| [LibreTexts](https://libretexts.org/) | Remixable textbook platform, 17 subject libraries | "3,000+ textbooks" (self-reported) | Mixed CC, per page | Breadth at lower-division level | Licence varies page by page; self-reported size inconsistent |

### DOAB

The [Directory of Open Access Books](https://directory.doabooks.org/) indexes peer-reviewed OA books and links to the full text. It is run by the OAPEN Foundation in The Hague ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directory_of_Open_Access_Books)). The dossier downloaded DOAB's complete metadata export on 2026-10-15 (a 281 MB CSV) and counted:

- **92,260 book records and 9,818 chapter records** from about 820 distinct publisher names (815–822, depending on how name variants are normalised).
- **Languages:** 58.0% English, 14.7% German, 13.1% French.
- **Growth:** about 7,200–8,200 books per publication year for 2020–2023, then about 5,100–5,300 for 2024 and 2025. The drop is very likely ingestion lag, not a real decline [I, medium].

Other published sizes count different things: "just over 60,000" titles in early 2023 ([Delta Think](https://www.deltathink.com/news-views-open-access-books-2), stale), "over 94,000" on the [Common Pile DOAB card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/common-pile/doab) (2025), and 128,242 OAI-PMH records, which include publisher, peer-review and deleted records.

**Subject mix.** 76.7% of books carry a Thema or BIC subject code. By first-listed code, classified books are 34.1% humanities and arts, 27.0% social sciences, economics and law, 28.7% STEM (science, maths, technology, computing, medicine), 6.9% reference and interdisciplinary, and 3.3% earth sciences, lifestyle and health. Counting any listed code instead, 34.7% carry a STEM code and 64.4% a humanities or social-science code. The mapping of codes to domains is the dossier's choice, so treat the split as roughly 60/30.

The technical core is thin. Counting a book once per code it carries: mathematics 451, probability and statistics 97, computer science 1,308, artificial intelligence 477, machine learning 74, programming 195, econometrics 25. For comparison: economics 2,509, philosophy 2,203, history 7,910.

**Three publishers dominate DOAB's STEM shelf.** Of 20,286 STEM books, IntechOpen supplies 6,449 (edited collections), MDPI 4,829 (reprints of journal special issues) and Frontiers 2,648 (topic collections): **68.6%** of the shelf, against 23.8% of DOAB overall. Next come KIT Scientific Publishing (1,681), Springer Nature (870) and Taylor & Francis (409); the MIT Press has 87. Of 115 DOAB titles containing "machine learning", 68 are MDPI. Only 96 DOAB titles contain "Introduction to" (49 in STEM), and 19 contain "Textbook". DOAB requires a peer-review policy from publishers but does not screen pedagogical quality.

**Licences.** CC BY 34.1%, CC BY-NC-ND 33.4%, none recorded 12.6%, other or publisher licence 6.7%, CC BY-NC 4.5%, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0%, CC BY-SA 3.7%, CC BY-ND 0.9%. So 37.8% allow commercial reuse. About 24,000 books are both English and CC BY, CC BY-SA or PD, which is roughly what the [Common Pile](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05209) training corpus took from DOAB. Licences are publisher-supplied, and Common Pile's card warns of "license laundering and inaccurate metadata".

**Good finds for this readership.** Below the edited collections, DOAB holds useful titles such as:

- MacAskill, Bykvist & Ord, *Moral Uncertainty* (OUP 2020, CC BY-NC-ND)
- *Essays on Longtermism* (OUP 2025, CC BY-NC)
- *An Anthology of Global Risk* (Open Book Publishers 2024, CC BY-NC) and *The Era of Global Risk* (OBP 2023)
- *Risk, Death, and Well-Being* (OUP 2025, CC BY-NC-ND)
- Halpern, *Actual Causality* (MIT 2016, CC BY-NC-ND)
- Schapire & Freund, *Boosting* (MIT 2012); Rasmussen & Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning* (MIT 2005); Bellemare, Dabney & Rowland, *Distributional Reinforcement Learning* (MIT 2023), all CC BY-NC-ND
- Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right* 4e (Springer 2024, CC BY-NC) and *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis* (Springer 2020)
- Barroso et al., *The Datacenter as a Computer* (Springer 2019, CC BY)
- *Learning Statistics with jamovi* (OBP 2025, CC BY-SA)

**If you browse DOAB for technical books, filter by publisher first.** Down-weight IntechOpen, MDPI and conference proceedings; up-weight university presses (Oxford, Cambridge, MIT, UCL, California, Michigan) and specialist OA presses (Open Book Publishers, Language Science Press, punctum). Without that filter, the STEM shelf is mostly special-issue reprints [I, high].

**Machine access.** The complete CSV export (`https://directory.doabooks.org/download-export?format=csv`) and the [OAI-PMH endpoint](https://directory.doabooks.org/oai/request?verb=Identify) both work from a cloud IP; the REST search API answered "You address is not allowed to access this API", and HTML record pages return 403 to scripts.

### OAPEN

The [OAPEN Library](https://library.oapen.org/) hosts the PDFs and EPUBs; 34,532 DOAB book records are harvested from it. Its export (112 MB CSV, 2026-10-15) has **36,434 books and 6,504 chapters from about 479 publishers**, 64% in English and 25% in German. Among classified books, 82.7% are humanities or social science and 10.6% STEM. The largest contributors are Taylor & Francis (4,427) and Springer Nature (3,705). The [OAPEN homepage](https://www.oapen.org/) claims "40,000+" OA books and "1.5 million+" monthly downloads, and announced a Max Planck Society collection on 2026-09-16. Machine access matches DOAB: CSV export and OAI-PMH work; REST search refuses cloud IPs.

For a technical reader OAPEN adds little that DOAB does not already list. It matters as the place the files live.

### OA programmes at presses

Counts are records in the DOAB and OAPEN exports (2026-10-15), so they are lower bounds for any publisher that does not deposit everything.

| Programme | Model | DOAB books | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Springer Nature OA books | Author or funder fee; mostly CC BY | 4,028 | 556 (2022), 607 (2023), 438 (2024), 395 (2025) deposited in OAPEN | Largest commercial OA book producer in these indexes; a handful of textbooks (Axler) |
| Taylor & Francis / Routledge | Author or funder fee | 3,821 | | Mostly HSS monographs and handbooks |
| MIT Press, incl. Direct to Open | Collective library funding, no author fees; launched 2021 | 280 | 79 DOAB records for 2022, 37 for 2023 | "80 monographs were made freely available in the program's second year"; "As of 2026, roughly 30% of the press's books … are open access" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Press), checked 2026-10-15; official pages blocked automated access) |
| Cambridge University Press | Author fees plus "Flip it Open" (titles opened after sales) | 416 | 1–3 per year in OAPEN | No programme figures found |
| Oxford University Press | Author or funder fee | 333 | 24–44 per year (2019–2025) | *Moral Uncertainty*, *Essays on Longtermism* |
| UCL Press | Fully OA university press | 396 | 25–50 per year | |
| Open Book Publishers | Library membership | 537 | 26–46 per year | Osborne & Rubinstein's *Models in Microeconomic Theory* |
| Other OA-heavy presses: ANU (fully OA), Michigan, punctum, UC Press Luminos, Language Science Press | Mixed: library support, membership, fees | 870, 670, 456, 301, 273 | 7–40 per year where measured | Almost entirely humanities, social science and linguistics |

University-press OA output is in the hundreds of titles per year, overwhelmingly humanities and social-science monographs. Programmes that systematically open STEM *textbooks* barely exist outside OpenStax-style OER and author-hosting [I]. The MIT Press is the exception that matters for this readership, because its OA list includes ML monographs such as *Boosting*, GPML and *Distributional RL*; the MIT titles in DOAB cited here are all CC BY-NC-ND.

### OpenStax

[OpenStax](https://openstax.org/) (Rice University, founded 2012) publishes peer-reviewed introductory textbooks. Its CMS API lists 129 book records on 2026-10-15: 84 live, 34 retired, 8 unlisted, 3 deprecated. Live titles have a median publish year of 2022. It self-reports 49 million students reached and \$3.8 billion saved all-time ([impact page](https://openstax.org/impact), undated).

**The licence switch.** On 2026-04-22 OpenStax announced: "OpenStax has transitioned our textbook library from a mix of CC BY and CC BY-NC-SA licensing to CC BY-NC-SA licensing across the library. This change will apply to all newly released and updated versions of our titles, with limited exceptions." The same post says "No action is needed by anyone who has previously created derivatives of CC BY content" ([OpenStax, 2026-04-22](https://openstax.org/blog/openstax-licensing)). The reasoning is in an earlier post: "Emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated this shift … permissive licensing has unintentionally rewarded those who are taking more than they invest" ([OpenStax, 2026-03-18](https://openstax.org/blog/when-open-resources-meet-a-changing-landscape)). On 2026-10-15 the API shows 70 of the 84 live titles under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 4 still under CC BY 4.0, and 10 with no licence field.

What this means:

- **For readers, nothing changes.** The books stay free online and as PDFs.
- **For commercial tools, new OpenStax content is off-limits without a deal.** Earlier CC BY versions remain reusable. If you depend on one, archive it now.
- **As a signal, it is the clearest case of an OER licence tightening because of AI.** I put about even odds on at least one other large OER producer moving new titles to a non-commercial licence by the end of 2027 [I, ~50%].

Titles relevant to this readership: *Statistics*, *Introductory Statistics* 2e, *Principles of Data Science* (2025), *Introduction to Python Programming* (2024), *Introduction to Computer Science* (2024), *Principles of Economics* 3e (2022) and *Introduction to Philosophy* (2022). None is graduate-level. The public CMS API (`https://openstax.org/apps/cms/api/v2/pages/?type=books.Book`) gives titles, states and dates without scraping.

### LibreTexts

[LibreTexts](https://libretexts.org/) is a remixable textbook platform with 17 subject libraries. Its homepage claims "3,000+ textbooks" and 500+ partner schools, while the same page also says "over 2000 textbooks" (self-reported, 2026). Licences are mixed Creative Commons, set per page, so check the licence of the exact page you plan to reuse. The Common Pile corpus extracted 62,269 CC BY, CC BY-SA or PD sections (5.3 GB) from it. Its remix model means the same chapter can appear in several "books". For this readership it is a lower-division reference, not a source of graduate texts [I, medium].

### Open Textbook Library

The [Open Textbook Library](https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks) (University of Minnesota, Open Education Network) is the best-curated catalog of open textbooks. The dossier harvested its full JSON API on 2026-10-15:

- **1,887 textbooks** (1,743 English, 107 Spanish). The API's `total_count` field says 2,015, but only 1,887 records are returned and the homepage says 1,887.
- **Recent:** median copyright year 2021; 58% from 2020 or later; 36% from 2023 or later.
- **Reviewed:** 64% have at least one faculty review, 7,581 reviews in all, mean rating 4.43 of 5. The high mean suggests a ceiling effect, so a rating is weak evidence of quality [I].
- **Licences:** CC BY-NC-SA 41.7%, CC BY 26.1%, CC BY-NC 18.3%, CC BY-SA 10.0%, CC BY-NC-ND 2.2%, GFDL 0.8%, CC0 0.8%.
- **Level:** mostly lower-division. Humanities 365, Social Sciences 249, Natural Sciences 216, Mathematics 163, Business 159, Computer Science 145, Economics 52, Philosophy 43, Statistics 34. Three titles have "Machine Learning" in the name; one is on game theory.

Other OER collections: the BCcampus Open Collection (Canadian post-secondary, mostly CC BY; its site refused automated access, but 44 of its titles appear in the OTL), and [OTexts](https://otexts.com/), which publishes Hyndman & Athanasopoulos's *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* 3e free online.

**Use the OTL when you need a reviewed introductory text in a field you do not know.** For graduate-level ML, statistics or decision theory it will rarely have what you want.

### The author-hosted canon

For a technical reader these are the most valuable free books. Few are in DOAB, because most are gratis rather than openly licensed. They exist because ML and statistics have a norm of author-hosting, and several publishers permit it: Cambridge (MacKay, Boyd, Barber, ROS, *Mathematics for ML*), MIT Press (Sutton & Barto, Mohri, Murphy, Prince), Springer (Bishop, ISL, ESL) and CRC (BDA3, and probably Blitzstein & Hwang).
