| Bishop, PRML | 41 | \$38.19 | \$38.19 |
| ESL 2e | 32 | \$42.14 | \$42.14 |
| DDIA 1e | 72 | \$44.54 | \$44.54 |
| BDA 3e | 39 | \$54.39 | \$54.39 |
| MacKay | 37 | \$56.21 | \$56.21 |
| *Statistical Rethinking* 2e | 37 | \$68.75 | \$68.75 |
| Jaynes | 32 | \$69.99 | \$69.99 |
| CLRS 4e | 63 | \$70.43 | \$70.43 |
| Sutton & Barto 2e | 39 | \$77.74 | \$77.74 |

What follows from these prices:

- **Older editions are the cheapest lever.** CLRS 3e costs 23% of the 4e price. For a reference text where the changes are minor, buy the older edition.
- **Cheap "new" textbooks are often international editions.** AIMA's \$33.15 listing against \$127.80 for the cheapest used copy fits that pattern [inferred]. The text is usually the same, but check exercises and page numbering if you are following a course.
- **AbeBooks beats ThriftBooks for exact editions.** ThriftBooks shows work-level "from" prices that can mix editions. On the same day it showed Goodfellow hardcovers from \$42.09 to \$100.00, PRML from \$66.39 and Jaynes at \$146.94, all above AbeBooks.
- **Bookshop.org sells new books, generally at list price [inferred].** It is a way to support independent stores, not a cheap route.
- **A copy you own works with any reading setup.** It is the one route here with no subscription to lapse and no platform terms on top. What you may do with it in an AI tool is a copyright question, covered in [The Legal Map](/building/legal-map/).

## What these licenses let you do with Claude

For anyone building reading tools, this table is the binding constraint.

| Service | Personal use only | Automated retrieval | AI input or prompting | AI training | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| O'Reilly (Individual, Teams, sponsored) | Yes; account sharing banned | Banned ("Web spiders … strictly prohibited") | **Banned** without the copyright owner's written permission | Banned | [Agreement, 2024-10-09](https://www.oreilly.com/membership-agreement/) |
| JSTOR (free account and JPASS) | Yes | Banned (no automated or systematic downloading) | Not addressed for outside tools; its AI-input clause covers JSTOR's own AI feature [unverified] | Banned ("to train large language models") | [Terms, 2026-04-24](https://about.jstor.org/terms/) |
| Springer+ | Yes; "not licensed for use by companies or organizations" | Not checked | Not checked | Not checked | [Springer+ support](https://support.springernature.com/en/support/solutions/articles/6000273908-what-is-springer-) |
| Perlego, Everand, Kindle Unlimited, Kobo Plus, DeepDyve | Personal subscriptions [inferred] | Not checked | Not checked | Not checked | n/a |

Three rules follow:

- **Treat every subscription as a reading license, not a corpus.** Build tools on catalog data (titles, tables of contents, subject placement), your own notes and highlights, and openly licensed text. Route the user to the licensed page; don't pipe the page into the model. [A Reference Architecture](/building/reference-architecture/) builds this in: its rights resolver ranks each access route, and only open or licensed items are fetched and parsed.
- **Personal licenses cannot be pooled.** A shared team tool cannot sit on one person's Springer+, O'Reilly Individual, Perlego or Everand account. The legitimate team path is an organizational license such as O'Reilly Teams or Enterprise. Even those probably exclude AI processing unless an addendum is negotiated, because sponsored users accept the same agreement [inferred, ~80%].
- **Bulk access gets noticed.** JSTOR reserves the right to suspend access per user or per IP address. Automated retrieval through an employer's proxy can cut off the whole organization.

## Which subscription to buy

| If you mainly read… | Buy | Skip | Why | Main obstacle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Practitioner ML, data and systems books, and a nearby library offers O'Reilly | **Nothing.** Get the card | O'Reilly Individual | The same platform at \$0. In the sample, the SFPL card plus free copies reached 28/33 | One in-person visit. Early releases and live events may be missing [inferred] |
| Practitioner books, with no library route | **O'Reilly** in monthly (\$49) or quarterly (\$129) bursts; annual (\$499) only if you will use all 12 months | Perlego | 14/33 against 5/33. O'Reilly, Pearson, Manning and Packt live there | Access ends when you stop paying. AI input banned |
| Theory texts in ML, statistics and CS (MIT Press, Cambridge, Springer, Pearson textbooks) | **No subscription.** Author PDFs, used copies, LAPL's Libby for MIT Press, and a Springer+ month for Springer monographs | O'Reilly, Perlego | Of 11 such texts in the sample, O'Reilly had 0 and Perlego 1. Free copies covered 7 (plus Jaynes in part); the cheapest listings for the other 4 were \$16–\$70 | Used shipping time. AIMA (\$128) and CS:APP (\$93) are expensive used |
| Monographs in humanities, social science, philosophy or economics | **Perlego Complete**: \$79 for 4 months for a project, \$199 a year if continuous | O'Reilly | 8/20 against 0/20, and deep Routledge, Cambridge and Princeton lists | US sales rights. Libraries had 16/20 of the famous titles anyway |
| Papers from the JSTOR backfile (economic history, philosophy, older statistics) | **Free JSTOR account**, then **JPASS** annual (\$199) once you need more than 10 a month or PDFs | DeepDyve | \$1.66 per PDF | Cap of 120 PDFs. No bulk or AI use |
| Paywalled STEM papers outside JSTOR, with no institution | The free workflow first. Then a **DeepDyve** month (\$59) for a heavy month, or a **Springer+ Basic** month for a Springer-heavy one | Pay-per-view | \$29.95–\$39.95 per item against \$59 flat | Streaming only, 40 printed pages a month. The \$25 Extension card beats both only if you want the course (about \$810+) anyway |
| Popular nonfiction (Kahneman, Tetlock, Ord) | **Library cards** through Libby | Everand, Kindle Unlimited | SFPL's Libby had 7 of 8 | Holds queues of weeks on bestsellers |
| Popular nonfiction, when holds queues are what limits you | **Everand Plus** (\$16.99 for 3 unlocks) | Everand Standard | \$5.66 against \$11.99 per book | Coverage unverified. A rental, not a purchase |
| Material for an AI reading tool | Whatever you would read anyway | Any subscription as a corpus | O'Reilly bans AI input; JSTOR bans LLM training and automated downloading | n/a |

**If you can buy only one:** if your library licenses O'Reilly, buy none and spend the money on used books. In the technical sample, the five titles the SFPL route missed (CLRS, AIMA, CS:APP, *GEB*, Jaynes) cost \$159 at the cheapest AbeBooks listings, or \$315 if AIMA and CS:APP are bought used rather than as cheap "new" copies: less than one year of O'Reilly, paid once, for books you keep. Without library O'Reilly, buy O'Reilly if your list is mostly practitioner books and Perlego Complete if it is mostly monographs. For a mixed list, use a library card for the O'Reilly half and a 4-month Perlego plan for each monograph-heavy project. No single subscription in the sample covered more than 42% of either list.

## Test coverage against your own list in an hour

The spot-check above is biased toward famous books. Your list is the only sample that matters. This protocol takes about an hour for 20–40 titles.

**Minutes 0–10: write the list.** Write 20–40 titles you expect to read in the next 12 months, one per line, as a distinctive title fragment ("Statistical Rethinking", "Seeing Like a State"). Include the obscure monographs you actually need; those are where libraries are weakest and subscriptions earn their price. Save the list as `my-list.txt`.

**Minutes 10–20: free copies.** Mark every title with a legal free copy, using the routes in [Open-Access Books and Textbooks](/access/open-books/) and [The Public Domain and Open Corpora](/access/public-domain/): author sites, open-access publisher editions, Open Library. In the technical sample this step alone covered a third of the list.

**Minutes 20–30: O'Reilly.** Download the public sitemap and match titles. The script takes about two minutes and makes about 30 requests. It reads only the public sitemap, not member content.

```bash
mkdir -p oreilly && cd oreilly
i=1; fails=0
while [ "$fails" -lt 2 ]; do      # the server sometimes returns 503; retry, stop after 2 misses
  if curl -sf --retry 4 --retry-delay 5 -o "p$i.xml" \
       "https://www.oreilly.com/epubs-books-p$i.xml"; then fails=0
  else rm -f "p$i.xml"; fails=$((fails+1)); fi
  i=$((i+1)); sleep 2
done
cat p*.xml | python3 -c '

t = sys.stdin.read()
pat = r"<loc>https://www\.oreilly\.com/library/view/[^/]+/([^/]+)/</loc>.*?<image:title>(.*?)</image:title>"
for id_, title in re.findall(pat, t):
    print(id_ + "\t" + html.unescape(title))' > titles.tsv
wc -l titles.tsv                          # 66,609 lines on 2026-10-15
# drop blank lines first: an empty pattern would match every title
grep -i -F -f <(grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' ../my-list.txt) titles.tsv   # id <TAB> title per hit
```

Check every hit by hand, because title matches give false positives. In the run for this chapter:

- "Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning" matched a 1992 Academic Press book (ID 9780120588305), not Bishop's.
- "Introduction to Algorithms" matched a Packt title (9781836203872), not CLRS.
- "Human Compatible" matched only the German edition.

The ID's ISBN prefix tells you the publisher. Don't match on print ISBNs. The sitemap uses e-book IDs, and none of the four print ISBNs tried appeared (DDIA, *Hands-On ML* 3e, *Statistical Rethinking* 2e and BDA3), although all four books are there.

**Minutes 30–40: your library cards.** In the Libby app, add every card you hold or could get, then search each remaining title, noting copies and holds. To script it, Libby's back end answers unauthenticated catalog queries such as `https://thunder.api.overdrive.com/v2/libraries/sfpl/media?query=designing%20data-intensive%20applications`. The response gives `ownedCopies`, `availableCopies` and `holdsCount` per title. On 2026-10-15 that query returned 10 owned copies, 2 available and 0 holds. The API is undocumented and may change, so rate-limit politely. Library keys and card eligibility are in [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/).

**Minutes 40–50: the paid catalogs.** For each remaining title:

- **Perlego:** search perlego.com from a US connection, open each hit's book page, and confirm it is readable in the US.
- **Everand:** use the 30-day web trial, which includes one unlock.
- **Kobo Plus:** use the 14-day US trial.
- **Springer and Cambridge:** search their sites. Springer, Apress and Palgrave chapters cost one Springer+ unit each. Cambridge sells only whole books and articles.
- **Papers:** search JSTOR (a hit there is not a guarantee of JPASS coverage), and use DeepDyve's free first month.

**Minutes 50–60: decide.** For each paid option S, count M(S): the titles S covers that free copies and your cards do not. Divide what S costs over the months you would actually read by M(S). Compare that with the used price of the same titles. Buy S only if its cost per marginal title is lower and you don't need to keep the books. Two worked examples from the technical sample:

- **O'Reilly Individual with an SFPL card:** M = 0 if the library edition carries the same books [~70%], so don't buy.
- **O'Reilly Individual without a library:** M = 10 over free copies. \$499 ÷ 10 is about \$50 per title, against \$32.74–\$68.75 used (mean \$48.68) for the three titles with checked prices. So the annual plan costs about the same as buying used and leaves you nothing to keep, while a two-month burst (\$98) to read three of them is cheaper than either.

Re-run the test yearly. Catalogs, sales rights and card rules changed repeatedly between 2024 and 2026.

## Open questions

- **O'Reilly's library edition.** Does "O'Reilly for Public Libraries" carry every book in the 66,609-title sitemap? Log in through an SFPL card and check a random sample of 50 sitemap titles, including early releases and translations.
- **Terms for library users.** Do library users accept the same membership agreement, AI-input clause included? Read the terms page shown at first library login.
- **Perlego's tiers.** Is the "restricted" flag (about 507,000 items) the Essential/Complete boundary? Search *Statistical Rethinking* and BDA3 from an Essential account.
- **AI clauses elsewhere.** What do the Perlego, Everand, Kindle Unlimited, Kobo Plus and DeepDyve terms say about AI input and automated access? Each is one careful read of a terms page.
- **Everand on a technical list.** What share of the 33-title technical list and the 20-title humanities list can Everand supply, and how many need unlocks? Run both lists during a 30-day web trial.
- **Kindle Unlimited and Kobo Plus.** What are the current US prices, plan names and borrowing caps, and how many titles from the 53-title lists does each carry? A logged-in browser session on each site answers the first part.
- **Perlego's long tail.** On a list of 30 recent specialist monographs (not famous books), how do Perlego and six Bay Area Libby collections compare? This tests the claim that Perlego's value lies outside the famous-book sample [~70%].
- **ACM membership.** Does it still bundle O'Reilly or other book access, a route widely cited around 2019–2024 [unverified]? What does it cost in 2026?
- **Springer+ scope.** Are Nature-branded journals unit-eligible? Search one Nature article while subscribed.
- **Holds against unlocks.** For the 10 most-held nonfiction titles at SFPL, what is the median wait? At what wait does an Everand unlock (\$5.66) become worth it for a reader who values time? Libby holds data polled daily would answer the first part.

## 9. Public Libraries
Source: https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/public-libraries/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. Eligibility rules, holdings, prices and statuses are as of 2026-10-15 unless another date is given; the card pages of all seven systems, Oakland's Link+ page and the Link+ member list were re-checked that day. Libby holdings come from a 53-title spot-check against OverDrive's public catalog API, not from logged-in tests; the per-library humanities breakdown was re-run on 2026-10-15 and matched R03's totals. Three points are unverified and flagged where they come up: whether SFPL's JSTOR link works from home, whether O'Reilly's library edition carries the full catalog, and whether LAPL's in-person cards give non-City residents the e-resources. Sources: the [R03 dossier](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/blob/main/apps/open-stacks/research/R03-paid-and-institutional-access.md) and primary sources linked inline.*

Library e-resource licenses are scoped to the population a library serves; LAPL says so explicitly (below). Most of California's big systems define that population as every California resident, so a Bay Area researcher can hold several overlapping sets of licenses for the price of a few desk visits. Whether the extra visits pay depends on what you read. For technical books, one SFPL card captured all the measured coverage. For humanities and trade books, the extra cards matter.

## The short version

- **Get a San Francisco Public Library (SFPL) card first.** It is free to every California resident: apply online, then show photo ID at any branch ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/welcome-new-cardholders), as of October 2026). Its O'Reilly login stands in for a \$499/year individual O'Reilly plan ([O'Reilly pricing](https://www.oreilly.com/pricing/), October 2026), if the library edition carries nearly all the books [~70%]. In a 33-book technical spot-check, SFPL's O'Reilly and Libby plus legal free copies covered **28/33 (85%)**.
- **For technical ebooks, the O'Reilly login is worth more than Libby.** O'Reilly held 14 of the 33 titles. SFPL's Libby held 10, mostly trade books (*Superforecasting*, *The Book of Why*).
- **Extra Bay Area cards raise humanities coverage, not technical coverage.** Across six Bay Area systems, Libby held **16/20 humanities titles** against SFPL's 10, and Santa Clara County was the best second card (+4). In the technical set the stack raised Libby's count from 10 to 18, but every added title was already readable through SFPL's O'Reilly login or a free copy, so coverage stayed at 28/33. For technical readers the extra cards buy format (Libby loans reach Kindle and Kobo e-readers; O'Reilly does not) and insurance if SFPL drops O'Reilly.
- **If you are not a California resident,** Santa Clara County Library District (SCCLD) gives a **free full-access card, including its 24/7 Online Library, to anyone with a US mailing address** who applies in person ([SCCLD](https://sccld.org/card/), October 2026). It is the only free Bay Area route for out-of-state readers I could confirm.
- **Out-of-area remote access is shrinking.** LAPL's instant e-card is now for Los Angeles City residents only, citing vendor licensing ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card/borrowing-policies-and-information)), and Orlando's Orange County Library System stopped issuing fee cards on 2026-07-31 ([OCLS](https://ocls.org/using-library/types-cards/what-are-types-cards/)). Get in-person cards while they are offered.
- **JSTOR through a public library is officially walk-in only** ([JSTOR](https://about.jstor.org/products/fees/public-libraries/)), yet SFPL and Berkeley list remote proxy links. I put it at [~50%] that an SFPL card gets you JSTOR from home. Test it before buying JPASS.
- **For print-only books, use Link+ before interlibrary loan, and both before buying.** Link+ reaches 11M+ items in 64 libraries, and most requests arrive in under a week ([Oakland PL](https://oaklandlibrary.org/borrow-from-another-library/)). Only 5 of the 64 members are academic libraries, so it is weaker for graduate texts.
- **Library access does not license AI use.** O'Reilly's membership agreement forbids using its content "as input or a prompt to a machine learning or AI system" ([O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/membership-agreement/), updated 2024-10-09). Read with the library login; give Claude your notes and the metadata.

## What a free SFPL card gets you

**Eligibility and process (as of 2026-10-15).** "Membership is free to all California residents." Apply online or on paper, then "present a valid photo ID in-person at any SFPL location" ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/welcome-new-cardholders)). No proof of address is asked. Californians without California ID can get a **Welcome card** (online resources, one physical item at a time) or, if they cannot verify their name, a **Digital Access card** ("full access to computers and online resources", no physical borrowing, one year). Visitors from outside California can buy a **Visitor card** with photo ID and a temporary California address: "Visitor cards cost \$10 and are valid for 3 months". Neither FAQ says whether the Visitor card includes e-resources ([SFPL FAQ](https://sfpl.libanswers.com/faq/129952); [SFPL FAQ](https://sfpl.libanswers.com/faq/65116)).

SFPL's A–Z database list has 228 entries over 23 pages ([SFPL Articles & Databases](https://sfpl.org/articles-databases), October 2026). The ones that matter for this wiki's readers:

| Resource | What you get | Catch | Replaces (prices as of Oct 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **O'Reilly for Public Libraries** | "50,000+ business and technology titles, 30,000+ hours of video" | Library-edition coverage of the full catalog is unverified (below). O'Reilly's AI-input ban probably applies | [O'Reilly Individual](https://www.oreilly.com/pricing/), \$499/yr |
| **Libby / OverDrive** (also Hoopla, Palace Project, Kanopy) | Ebooks and audiobooks on loan. In the spot-check, 10/33 technical and 10/20 humanities titles | Holds queues on popular books | Buying the ebook |
| **LinkedIn Learning** | 16,000+ courses | — | A LinkedIn Learning subscription |
| **Udemy (Gale Presents)** | 4,000+ courses | A curated subset of Udemy [inference] | Per-course Udemy purchases |
| **ProQuest eBook Central** | Academic ebook aggregator | Remote access not separately confirmed [~80% it works through the library login] | Publisher ebook purchases |
| **EBSCO eBook Collection** | Academic ebooks | **Main Library only** | — |
| **Academic Search Complete** (EBSCO), **Gale Academic OneFile** | Multidisciplinary article databases | Thin for ML and statistics; stronger for social science and humanities journals [~65%, inference] | Pay-per-view articles |
| **JSTOR** | Listed behind SFPL's EZproxy login | JSTOR says public-library access is walk-in only. Remote use [~50%] | [JPASS](https://about.jstor.org/products/jpass/), \$199/yr for 120 PDFs |
| **Statista, IBISWorld, Morningstar** | Market statistics, industry reports, fund and equity data | Statista requires card number plus PIN from 2026-04-01 | Commercial subscriptions |
| **NYT, WSJ, Washington Post, PressReader** | Newspapers and magazines | — | News subscriptions |
| Also: OED, WorldCat, Treehouse | Reference; programming courses | — | — |

Resource names and descriptions are from SFPL's A–Z list as of 2026-10-15 ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/articles-databases)); the Catch and Replaces columns are mine.

**What it covers.** Checked against 33 well-known technical books (DDIA, *Hands-On ML*, CLRS, Goodfellow, PRML, *Statistical Rethinking*, BDA3, Jaynes, *Superforecasting* and others):

| Route | Titles (n = 33) | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Legal free full text (author sites, open licenses) | 11 (+1 partial) | 33% |
| O'Reilly (via the public sitemap) | 14 | 42% |
| SFPL Libby | 10 | 30% |
| SFPL O'Reilly ∪ SFPL Libby | 21 | 64% |
| **SFPL card + legal free copies** | **28** | **85%** |
| Missing | CLRS, AIMA, CS:APP, *Gödel, Escher, Bach*, full Jaynes | — |

Source: the R03 spot-check, 2026-10-15. The counts are primary lookups; the unions are mine. The sample is small, hand-picked and biased toward famous books. Treat 85% as an upper estimate, not a measured rate: a less famous list will score lower [~70%; inference]. For humanities and social science the same card covered 10/20 titles, and O'Reilly contributed nothing (0/20).

### O'Reilly through the library

- **The catalog is narrower than its reputation.** O'Reilly's public book sitemap lists 66,609 title URLs as of 2026-10-15 ([sitemap](https://www.oreilly.com/book-sitemap.xml)). By ISBN prefix, roughly 9,200 are Wiley; 9,000 O'Reilly (about 2,900 of them translations); 6,200 Pearson/Addison-Wesley; 4,000 Apress; 3,000 CRC/Taylor & Francis; 1,500 De Gruyter; and 1,100 Manning. Packt's ISBN range holds at most 6,443 (about 4,700 in identifiable Packt blocks). There are **zero MIT Press, Cambridge, Oxford or core Springer titles**, so no CLRS, Goodfellow, Sutton & Barto or PRML. (The prefix-to-publisher mapping is inferred, as corrected in R03's verification pass.)
- **Library edition versus full catalog.** SFPL's blurb says "50,000+" titles against 66,609 sitemap entries, of which about 1,300 are probably video or audio. Early-release books and live events may be excluded. I put it at [~70%] that nearly all *books* in the sitemap are readable through the library; nobody in this research logged in to check.
- **One O'Reilly card is enough.** Oakland, Berkeley ("O'Reilly Technical Books"), San José and Santa Clara County also list O'Reilly ([Oakland](https://oaklandlibrary.org/resource/), [Berkeley](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/explore/elibrary/alphabetical-list), [San José](https://www.sjpl.org/eresources/), [SCCLD](https://sccld.org/online-library/)). If the library editions are the same product, a second O'Reilly login adds nothing [~85%] except a backup if one library drops the license.
- **The terms probably bind you.** O'Reilly's membership agreement (updated 2024-10-09) bans "Web spiders" and AI training. It forbids storing or transmitting content "as input or a prompt to a machine learning or AI system" without "the express prior written permission of the copyright owner", and it caps quotes at 250 words ([O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/membership-agreement/), checked 2026-10-15). Users who reach the service through a Sponsor's agreement are bound by the same agreement plus any terms the Sponsor adds. The agreement does not mention libraries. I infer that library patrons count as sponsored users [~75%]. If so, pasting an O'Reilly chapter into Claude breaches the contract. See [The Legal Map](/building/legal-map/).

**Decision.** If you were going to pay \$499/year for O'Reilly and you live in California, get the SFPL card instead. Pay only if you need what the Individual plan includes and the library edition may lack (early-release books, live events, interactive labs and sandboxes; [O'Reilly pricing](https://www.oreilly.com/pricing/), October 2026) or have no eligible library. Cloud labs are a Teams feature, not part of the Individual plan.

### JSTOR and the article databases

- JSTOR's fee page for public libraries says: "Remote access for public libraries is not currently supported" and "JSTOR for public libraries is limited to walk-in access" ([JSTOR](https://about.jstor.org/products/fees/public-libraries/), checked 2026-10-15).
- SFPL's database list nonetheless links JSTOR through `ezproxy.sfpl.org`, and Berkeley PL lists JSTOR/Artstor behind its own EZproxy login ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/articles-databases); [Berkeley PL](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/explore/elibrary/alphabetical-list)).
- LAPL marks JSTOR "Only available at LAPL Locations" ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/digital-library/search)).

Possible explanations: a legacy agreement, a proxy restricted to in-library IP addresses, or a stale listing. I put it at [~50%] that SFPL's link works from home. Even a working link may reach only part of JSTOR: public libraries can license the full archive or individual packages such as Collection I (arts and sciences) and Collection III (primary sources) ([JSTOR](https://about.jstor.org/products/fees/public-libraries/)). Test it with your own card before buying JPASS. If it fails, JSTOR's free account still gives 10 articles every 30 days, read online; see [Open Papers and Preprints](/access/open-papers/).

**Physics journals at Oakland and Berkeley.** Both list American Physical Society journals. Berkeley PL labels *Physical Review* "in library access only". Oakland links straight to journals.aps.org with no proxy login, so access is probably walk-in only as well ([Berkeley PL](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/explore/elibrary/alphabetical-list); [Oakland](https://oaklandlibrary.org/resource/), October 2026). That makes them a free walk-in route to APS journals; whether it works on your own laptop over library Wi-Fi was not checked.

**Expectations for papers.** Public-library article databases are general-purpose aggregators. For ML, statistics and forecasting papers, the legal open-access cascade (arXiv, Unpaywall, author copies) will usually beat them [~70%, inference]. They earn their place for social-science and humanities journals and for newspapers and trade press. University routes cover the rest: see [University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/).

## The other Bay Area systems

Each system below gives California residents a free card. They differ in how you prove eligibility and in what they add to SFPL. Libby increments are over SFPL alone, from the spot-check samples (2026-10-15).

| Library | Eligibility (Oct 2026) | How to get it | What it adds beyond SFPL | Card life |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oakland PL** | Free to California residents | Apply online. The unverified card gives "most electronic resources" at once but expires in 30 days. Oakland, Emeryville and Piedmont residents can verify by phone or email; everyone else verifies with ID at a branch ([OPL](https://oaklandlibrary.org/get-a-library-card/)) | APS journals (probably in-library only); Pressbooks; backup O'Reilly ([OPL A–Z](https://oaklandlibrary.org/resource/)). Its Libby added no titles in either sample | 3 years |
| **Berkeley PL** | "Library cards are free to all California residents" | "Applicants must be present." Photo ID and address verification. An Easy Access card for people who cannot verify an address needs photo ID only, gives full access to online databases and up to three physical items, and lasts 1 year ([BPL](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/library/your-card)) | JSTOR/Artstor via EZproxy; *Physical Review* (in-library). Libby: 0 technical, +2 humanities. **Libby and Kanopy logins need card number plus PIN from 2026-10-15** ([BPL](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/)) | 4 years; an expired card is renewed in person |
| **San José PL** | Full Access card "Available to California residents" | Apply online, then pick up at any branch with "proof of California address and a valid photo ID" ([SJPL](https://www.sjpl.org/membership/)) | Libby: **+6 technical**, 0 humanities; 250+ Great Courses in Libby; backup O'Reilly ([SJPL eResources](https://www.sjpl.org/eresources/)) | 4 years; renewable in person |
| **Santa Clara County Library District** | eCard "instantly" for county residents. **Free Full Access card for anyone with a US mailing address**, at a visit | Fill in the online application from inside the library, then go to the Accounts Desk with ID "showing your picture, name, and proof of your current address" ([SCCLD](https://sccld.org/card/)) | Libby: +2 technical, **+4 humanities** (the best second card for humanities); The Great Courses; EBSCO and Gale reference ebooks; backup O'Reilly ([SCCLD](https://sccld.org/online-library/)) | Not stated |
| **Peninsula Library System** (San Mateo County Libraries and the city libraries of Burlingame, Daly City, Menlo Park, Redwood City, San Mateo, South San Francisco and San Bruno) | The card page states no California-residency rule. People outside San Mateo County are told to pick the most convenient library | Register online, then finish in person with "picture identification and proof of current home address". The new online account expires in 90 days ([PLS](https://plsinfo.org/get-a-library-card/)) | Libby: +2 technical, +1 humanities | Not stated |

San José also issues a Limited Status card for people who cannot show proof of address. It offers "online resources anytime, anywhere" and one physical item at a time ([SJPL](https://www.sjpl.org/membership/)). The page does not say which licensed e-resources it includes.

### The Libby card-stack effect

Libby searches all your cards together, and each library buys its own ebook copies. The R03 spot-check queried OverDrive's catalog for each title at each library on 2026-10-15 and counted ebook editions with at least one owned copy ([OverDrive Thunder API example](https://thunder.api.overdrive.com/v2/libraries/sfpl/media?query=designing%20data-intensive%20applications)). The humanities column was broken out by library in a re-run the same day, with the same criterion; its totals (10, 16, 19) match R03's.

| Cards in Libby (cumulative) | Technical, Libby only (n = 33) | Technical, with SFPL O'Reilly + free copies | Humanities and social science (n = 20) |
|---|---|---|---|
| SFPL alone | 10 | 28 | 10 |
| + San José | 16 | 28 | 10 |
| + Santa Clara County | 17 | 28 | 14 |
| + Peninsula | 18 | 28 | 15 |
| + Berkeley | 18 | 28 | 16 |
| **+ Oakland (all six Bay Area systems)** | **18** | **28** | **16** |
| **+ LAPL** | **23** | **29** | **19** |
| + NYPL, Brooklyn | 23 (no gain) | 29 | not checked |

Increments are order-dependent; each row credits shared titles to the libraries above it. Technical: San José added *Hands-On ML*, *Designing ML Systems*, *AI Engineering*, *The Rust Programming Language*, *The Pragmatic Programmer* and *SICP*; Santa Clara County added *How to Measure Anything* (SFPL has only the audiobook); Peninsula added Raschka's *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)*. Humanities: Santa Clara County added Kuhn's *Structure*, Anderson's *Imagined Communities*, Simler and Hanson's *The Elephant in the Brain* and Mokyr's *A Culture of Growth*; Peninsula added Polanyi's *The Great Transformation*; Berkeley added Rawls. Oakland added nothing in either sample (it holds several of these titles only as audiobooks). Hacking's *The Emergence of Probability* was missing everywhere. Matching was automatic (title plus author), so a few false negatives are possible.

**What the stack is worth.** All eight technical titles the Bay Area cards added were already on O'Reilly or free online, which is why the middle column never moves. For a technical reader the extra cards buy two things: Libby editions, which reach Kindle and Kobo e-readers where O'Reilly cannot (below), and a fallback if SFPL drops its O'Reilly license. For a humanities reader the stack is a real gain, 10 to 16 of 20, and most of it comes from Santa Clara County.

**What LAPL adds.** LAPL holds MIT Press ebooks that no Bay Area system had: CLRS (3e and 4e, 3 copies each), Goodfellow's *Deep Learning* (3) and Sutton & Barto (1), plus Pearson's *Clean Code* and Manning's *Deep Learning with Python*. The R03 verification pass re-confirmed the MIT Press holdings. But Goodfellow and Sutton & Barto are free online, and *Clean Code* and Chollet are on O'Reilly, so LAPL's net technical gain is one title, CLRS (28 to 29 of 33). A used CLRS 3e cost \$16.25 shipped on 2026-10-15 ([AbeBooks](https://www.abebooks.com/servlet/SearchResults?isbn=9780262033848&sortby=17)). LAPL's larger gains are humanities (+3 of 20 over the Bay stack: Parfit's *Reasons and Persons*, Weber's *Protestant Ethic*, Popper's *Logic of Scientific Discovery*) and its research databases (below). **Decision:** get an LAPL card on your next trip to Los Angeles. It is not worth a dedicated trip for technical reading.

**Holds are the real price.** A snapshot on 2026-10-15:

| Title | Library | Copies | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Thinking, Fast and Slow* | SFPL | 13 | 51 |
| *Thinking, Fast and Slow* | LAPL | 16 | 87 |
| *Guns, Germs, and Steel* | LAPL | 7 | 35 |
| *Thinking in Systems* | SFPL / LAPL | 26 / 18 | 14 / 30 |
| *AI Engineering* | LAPL / San José | 6 / 5 | 16 / 9 |
| *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)* | LAPL | 3 | 20 |
| *The Alignment Problem* | SFPL | 7 | 8 |
| *Human Compatible* | SFPL | 2 | 9 |

A rough estimate of the wait for a new hold is (holds ÷ copies) × loan length. For *Thinking, Fast and Slow* at SFPL that is 51 ÷ 13 ≈ 3.9 loan periods: about 8 weeks at 14-day loans or 12 at 21-day loans, if every borrower keeps the book for the full term. Early returns and skipped holds shorten the real wait; pickup windows lengthen it [inference; I did not check SFPL's loan lengths]. With holds at several libraries, your wait is roughly the *minimum* of the queues [inference], which is where the card stack pays off for popular trade books. The stack does nothing for a title no library licenses, like *Gödel, Escher, Bach*, which may have no ebook edition.

**Unusual licenses.** Santa Clara County showed **334 copies** of the *AI Engineering* audiobook, 333 of them available, and San José showed 50 copies of a *Pragmatic Programmer* ebook edition, 49 available ([Thunder API](https://thunder.api.overdrive.com/v2/libraries/sanjose/media?query=the%20pragmatic%20programmer), 2026-10-15). Counts like these suggest cost-per-circulation or simultaneous-use licenses [~70%], so some technical titles may never have queues at some libraries.

**Reading Libby loans on e-ink.** Kindles receive Libby loans only through Libby's "Send to Kindle (U.S. only)" ([Libby on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.overdrive.mobile.android.libby)). Kobo readers have OverDrive built in. Of the mainstream e-ink lines, only Android tablets (Boox) run both Libby and the O'Reilly app; Kindle and Kobo cannot run O'Reilly. Details are in [Reading Modes and Devices](/environments/reading-modes-and-devices/).

### LAPL's research databases

An LAPL card is free to California residents, collected in person in Los Angeles after optional online pre-registration ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card)). LAPL lists 200+ databases and 1.5M+ ebooks and audiobooks. For researchers the notable ones are **ProQuest Central**, ProQuest Research Library, ABI/Inform, **OECD iLibrary**, **HeinOnline**, Lexis Advance, Westlaw, Oxford Reference, Gale eBooks and LinkedIn Learning. JSTOR is in-library only, and **there is no O'Reilly** ([LAPL research databases](https://lapl.org/digital-library/research); [LAPL resource list](https://lapl.org/digital-library/search), October 2026). I did not check which databases work remotely.

LAPL's pages say "Licensing agreements with our digital content vendors require that only Los Angeles City residents can receive an e-card" ([LAPL borrowing policies](https://lapl.org/library-card/borrowing-policies-and-information), checked 2026-10-15). They do not say whether a full card issued in person to a Californian living outside the City includes Libby and remote databases. Since the restriction is worded about e-cards, I put it at [~80%] that it does. Ask at the desk when you collect the card.

## Out-of-area access is shrinking

The standard advice used to be: buy a fee card from a big library in another state, or get LAPL's instant e-card, and read remotely. Both routes are narrowing.

| Library | Route | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LAPL** | Instant e-card | **Los Angeles City residents only**, per vendor licensing. I could not date the change | [LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card/borrowing-policies-and-information) |
| LAPL | Full card | Free to California residents; **\$50 for applicants outside California**, issued and renewed in person only | same |
| **Orange County Library System (Orlando, FL)** | National fee card, which had included remote databases and ebook holds | "No longer being issued or renewed, as of July 31, 2026" | [OCLS](https://ocls.org/using-library/types-cards/what-are-types-cards/) |
| San Antonio PL | Bexar County residents outside city limits | New **\$30/year** fee from 2026-10-01, paid in person | [SAPL](https://guides.mysapl.org/librarycards) |
| **Santa Clara County Library District** | Any US mailing address | **Free full card, in person** (counter-example) | [SCCLD](https://sccld.org/card/) |
| SFPL | Visitor card for visitors from outside California (photo ID plus a temporary California address) | \$10 for 3 months; e-resource access not stated | [SFPL FAQ](https://sfpl.libanswers.com/faq/129952) |
| Brooklyn PL, Free Library of Philadelphia, Fairfax County | Fee cards | **Could not verify**: the sites returned 403/404 to automated requests on 2026-10-15. From pre-2026 knowledge, not re-checked, Brooklyn and Philadelphia sold non-resident cards for about \$50/year [unverified, low confidence] | — |

All statuses are as of 2026-10-15.

**The pattern.** E-content vendors increasingly tie licenses to the population a library serves. LAPL says so explicitly, and JSTOR's walk-in-only public-library model applies the same logic to databases. Libraries are closing the remote-only, out-of-area routes first. I put it at [~70%] that at least one more widely recommended non-resident or e-card route in the US closes or narrows by the end of 2027. The evidence is thin: two closures (LAPL's e-card restriction and OCLS) and one new fee (San Antonio) in a single snapshot, no trend data, and several pages that could not be checked.

**What to do about it.**

- Get in-person cards while they are offered, and renew before they lapse. Several renewals need a visit: Berkeley (expired cards), LAPL's non-resident card, and Oakland's unverified online card, which cannot be renewed online.
- Do not build a reading workflow on a single remote-only fee card.
- If you live outside California and visit the Bay Area, get the SCCLD card. If you visit Los Angeles from outside California, LAPL's \$50 card is the paid option.
- Keep your own list of routes with last-verified dates and re-check it yearly; this table will go stale.

## Link+ and interlibrary loan

Libby covers ebooks. For print-only books (no ebook edition, or no library license), California's public libraries have two lending networks.

| Route | Reach | Limits and costs (Oct 2026) | Speed | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Link+** | "over 11 million items from 64 libraries throughout California and Nevada" (Oakland's description). The member list shows 64 libraries, all in California (three marked "coming soon"): 59 public and 5 academic (Santa Clara University, Loyola Marymount, Pacific Union College, Napa Valley College, Solano Community College) | Oakland: 21-day loans with one 21-day renewal; no late fees; **\$115** for a lost or significantly damaged item. Berkeley PL: up to **25** Link+ items at once, 21 days, renewable once. SFPL participates (one renewal, 3 weeks) | "Most LINK+ requests arrive in less than one week" | [Oakland](https://oaklandlibrary.org/borrow-from-another-library/); [Link+ members](https://csul.iii.com/screens/members.html); [Berkeley PL](https://www.berkeleypubliclibrary.org/explore/linkplus); [SFPL FAQ](https://sfpl.libanswers.com/faq/85266) |
| **Interlibrary loan (Oakland PL)** | Books and journal articles from libraries outside Link+ | **3 requests per month.** Excludes current-year books, items Oakland owns, anything available through Link+, and DVDs, CDs and audiobooks. "Not all materials are available for free"; the library checks with you before accepting a charge. \$115 minimum for a lost item | Not stated | [Oakland](https://oaklandlibrary.org/borrow-from-another-library/) |
| UC Berkeley and Stanford paid community cards | — | **Exclude** interlibrary borrowing | — | See [University and Employer Access](/access/academic-and-employer/) |

**Order of operations for a print-only book.**

1. Search your home library's catalog, then request through Link+. It is free and usually takes under a week; Berkeley PL lets you borrow up to 25 Link+ items at once.
2. If Link+ has nothing, use interlibrary loan. It is rationed (3 a month at Oakland) and sometimes charged, so save it for things Link+ cannot supply, journal articles included.
3. If you will annotate the book or need it for more than six weeks, buy used. On 2026-10-15 the cheapest shipped AbeBooks copies of the spot-check's residual titles were *Gödel, Escher, Bach* \$8.23, AIMA 4e \$33.15 (new, probably an international edition), CS:APP 3e \$31.54 (new) and Jaynes \$69.99 ([AbeBooks](https://www.abebooks.com/servlet/SearchResults?isbn=9780521592710&sortby=17)).

I did not check which Link+ libraries hold those residual titles. Because Link+ is almost all public libraries, expect it to be weaker for graduate texts like Jaynes or CS:APP than for trade books [~70%, inference]; that is where an interlibrary-loan request or a university walk-in visit earns its place.

## Get the cards that matter in one afternoon

The six Bay Area systems split into two loops: the Peninsula and South Bay (Peninsula Library System, San José, Santa Clara County) and the East Bay (Oakland, Berkeley). The Peninsula–South Bay loop supplied all eight extra technical Libby titles and five of the six extra humanities titles. After that loop, the East Bay added one more (Rawls, at Berkeley), plus Berkeley's JSTOR/Artstor link and both libraries' in-library physics journals.

- **Technical reader, reading on a laptop or Boox:** SFPL alone gives the measured coverage. The loop is optional.
- **Technical reader on Kindle or Kobo:** add San José, for Libby editions of six titles otherwise available only through O'Reilly or the free web.
- **Humanities reader, or a reader from outside California:** add Santa Clara County first (+4 humanities titles; the only card confirmed open to any US address).
- **Time for the full loop:** do SFPL plus the Peninsula–South Bay loop, and the East Bay another day.

**Costs.** For a California resident every card is **\$0** plus transit. For a non-Californian, only SCCLD is confirmed free; PLS states no residency rule; the others require California residence (as of 2026-10-15).

**The night before (about 30 minutes).**

1. **SFPL:** submit the online application ([SFPL](https://sfpl.org/welcome-new-cardholders)).
2. **Oakland:** apply online ([OPL](https://oaklandlibrary.org/get-a-library-card/)). You can use most of its e-resources at once. The card expires in 30 days unless you verify it; outside Oakland, Emeryville and Piedmont that means a branch visit.
3. **San José:** submit the online application ([SJPL](https://www.sjpl.org/membership/)).
4. **Peninsula Library System:** register online and pick the member library on your route ([PLS](https://plsinfo.org/get-a-library-card/)). The new account expires in 90 days if you do not finish in person.
5. **LAPL:** pre-register for your next trip to Los Angeles ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card)).
6. **Documents:** photo ID plus proof of current address (a California address for San José). SFPL needs only the photo ID.

**The afternoon, Peninsula–South Bay loop (by car is simplest).** Increments are cumulative in this order.

| Stop | What to bring | You leave with | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Any SFPL branch | Photo ID | O'Reilly, Libby, LinkedIn Learning, Udemy, ProQuest eBook Central, EBSCO and Gale databases, JSTOR link, newspapers, Link+ | \$0 |
| 2. A Peninsula Library System member library | Photo ID + proof of address | Libby card #2: +2 technical, +1 humanities | \$0 |
| 3. Any San José PL branch | Photo ID + proof of California address | Libby card #3: +5 technical, 0 humanities; backup O'Reilly | \$0 |
| 4. Any SCCLD branch (for example Milpitas or Cupertino) | Photo ID with current address | Libby card #4: +1 technical, +4 humanities; The Great Courses; backup O'Reilly | \$0 |

The order can run in either direction. Check each branch's hours before you go.

**The East Bay loop (another afternoon, by BART).** Oakland's Main Library, to verify the online card if you live outside Oakland, Emeryville and Piedmont, and Berkeley's Central Library, where "applicants must be present". Both are near BART stations. Go for the in-library physics journals, Berkeley's JSTOR/Artstor link and Rawls; beyond the first loop, neither library added other titles in the samples. **Total for six Bay Area cards: \$0 plus fares.** Add LAPL (\$0 for Californians) on any trip to Los Angeles.

**The evening after (about 45 minutes).**

1. **Add every card to Libby.** Berkeley PL requires a PIN for Libby from 2026-10-15, so set one when you get that card. Turn on hold notifications.
2. **Activate O'Reilly once,** from the link on SFPL's database list.
3. **Set the SFPL PIN** if you want Statista (required from 2026-04-01).
4. **Test JSTOR from home** through SFPL's link and record whether it works. That settles a [~50%] question for your own planning.
5. **Place holds at every library** that has a book you want, and take the first copy that arrives.
6. **Put the expiry dates in your calendar:** Oakland 3 years; Berkeley and San José 4 years; Oakland online card 30 days if unverified; PLS online registration 90 days.

**Expected payoff.** If your reading resembles the spot-check samples: about 85% of a technical list (with legal free copies; SFPL alone gets you there) and about 80% of a humanities list as ebooks (this needs the stack), at \$0, with weeks of holds on popular trade titles. The remainder goes to Link+, interlibrary loan, [cheap subscriptions](/access/subscriptions/) such as Perlego for academic monographs (Bay Area Libby plus Perlego reached 18/20 humanities titles), or a used copy. The [Access Ladder](/access/access-ladder/) puts these routes in order.

## For tool builders

Public libraries are the largest free *content* source for a personal catalog that routes each work to wherever it can be read. They are also the most tightly licensed.

- **Availability data is reachable.** The Libby back end (OverDrive's undocumented "Thunder" catalog API) returns owned copies, available copies and holds count per title per library. Library keys found by R03: `sfpl`, `oakland`, `berkeleypubliclibrary`, `sanjose`, `santaclara`, `pls`, `lapl`, `nypl`, `brooklyn`. `berkeley` is Berkeley Law's library, not Berkeley PL. Ebook records can show zero owned copies and a holds queue (Oakland's *Guns, Germs, and Steel* ebook did on 2026-10-15), so filter on owned copies, not on the record's presence. The API is undocumented and may change; query it at polite rates. R09 rates scraping public-library catalogs **yellow**: facts are free, but terms of service still bind, so use APIs, rate-limit and honor robots.txt ([The Legal Map](/building/legal-map/)).
- **Two small modeling problems.** Choosing cards (and month-long subscription bursts) for a reading list is weighted set cover; the card-stack table above is a hand-run instance. Forecasting holds is a queueing problem: poll copies and holds daily, publish "P(available within 7 days)" per title per library, and score it with Brier scores against actual pickup dates.
- **Route to the content; do not ingest it.** O'Reilly forbids AI input. JSTOR's terms (2026-04-24) ban "systematically" downloading and using content "to train large language models" ([JSTOR terms](https://about.jstor.org/terms/)). A catalog can show "Libby SJPL, 0 holds" or "O'Reilly via SFPL" and deep-link there. The licensed text stays behind the library login. See [A Reference Architecture](/building/reference-architecture/) for the license-firewall layer.

## Open questions

- **Does SFPL's JSTOR EZproxy link work from home?** A cardholder can test it in five minutes. If it does, is it full JSTOR or one of the packages JSTOR sells public libraries (Collection I, II or III)?
- **Is O'Reilly for Public Libraries the full book catalog?** Sample 200 ISBNs from the sitemap and check each through a library login. The current estimate is [~70%] that nearly all books are included.
- **Do LAPL's in-person cards give non-City Californians Libby and remote databases?** Ask LAPL or test with a card. The estimate is [~80%] yes.
- **Does the O'Reilly membership agreement bind library patrons verbatim,** or do library-access terms differ? Find the library-edition terms page or ask a library's e-resources librarian.
- **What do SFPL's \$10 Visitor card and SJPL's Limited Status card include?** Specifically, do they reach Libby and O'Reilly? Both could matter to visitors from out of state.
- **How well do the hand-picked samples predict coverage?** Replace both sets with a random sample of a few hundred titles drawn from syllabi, and re-run the per-library breakdown, to measure coverage without fame bias.
- **How well does the holds-queue arithmetic predict real waits?** Log hold dates and pickup dates across a few dozen holds and compare them with Libby's own estimates and with (holds ÷ copies) × loan length.
- **Which Link+ libraries hold the residual print-only titles** (Jaynes, CS:APP, AIMA, *Gödel, Escher, Bach*)? A Link+ catalog search answers it, and tests whether a mostly public network covers graduate texts.
- **Do Brooklyn PL and the Free Library of Philadelphia still sell non-resident cards with e-access,** and at what price? Both blocked automated checks; a manual visit to their pages resolves it.

------------------------------------------------------------
## 10. University and Employer Access
Source: https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/academic-and-employer/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. Prices, eligibility rules and product statuses are as of 2026-10-15 unless another date is given; every university, alumni-association and publisher page cited was re-checked that day. Unverified and flagged inline: whether Extension's "Start Anytime" courses qualify for the \$25 library card, whether non-alumni Cal Alumni Association members get alumni benefits, what UC Berkeley's publisher licenses say about AI, Stanford's visiting-scholar fees, and IEEE and ACM corporate pricing. Sources: the [R03 dossier](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/blob/main/apps/open-stacks/research/R03-paid-and-institutional-access.md), the [R09 dossier](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/blob/main/apps/open-stacks/research/R09-legal-and-licensing.md) for license terms, and primary sources linked inline.*

A university library holds what public libraries and consumer subscriptions don't: the big publishers' full journal backfiles, specialist databases, and stacks of out-of-print monographs. Publisher licenses decide who may use them, and for remote access the answer is nearly always "current affiliates". This chapter covers what is still open to everyone else in the Bay Area, what the paid routes cost once you include the price of becoming eligible, and how the same licensing logic binds access through an employer.

## The short version

- **Walk-in access is free and underused.** As of October 2026, any visitor to UC Berkeley's libraries can use licensed databases on the libraries' public computers ([UC Berkeley Library](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visitors)). SF State's public research stations need "no account or login" ([accounts](https://library.sfsu.edu/accounts)), and "you can download and save information to a personal USB drive" ([community borrowers](https://library.sfsu.edu/community-borrowers)). Stanford gives anyone 7 free day passes a year, 14 for its alumni ([Stanford Libraries](https://library.stanford.edu/about-stanford-libraries/visitor-access)). For a few dozen paywalled papers in journals the library licenses, one planned half-day at a terminal beats any subscription.
- **No paid community card includes remote e-resources.** That holds for UC Berkeley's \$100 California-resident card, Stanford's \$35–\$1,000 researcher cards and SF State's \$50 community card. They buy building entry and borrowing.
- **The UC Berkeley Extension card does include remote access, but the real price is the course.** The card is \$25 for six months, but you must be registered in a "semester-length (10+ week)" Extension course ([Extension help center](https://berkeleyextension.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16655644122647-Library-use), updated 2026-09-16). In a sample of 76 open online sections on 2026-10-15, courses of 2 or more units cost \$665–\$2,100. The cheapest 3-unit course, the cheapest likely to qualify, was \$810. Budget about \$835 per six months, and take this route only if you want the course anyway.
- **A visiting-scholar appointment is the cheapest full remote access if you have a sponsor.** It costs \$750 for the first year and \$1,500 for a consecutive second year. It needs a department appointment and a faculty sponsor, and the norm is a PhD ([VSPA fee](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/about/university-services-fee); [exception rules](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/staff-faculty/vsvsr-appointment-exceptional-request-guidelines)).
- **For physical research-library books, UC Berkeley's \$100 card is the value option.** It covers 20 books at a time and the Main (Gardner) Stacks ([UC Berkeley Library](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/find/borrow-renew)). Stanford charges \$1,000 a year for the equivalent. None of these cards includes interlibrary loan.
- **Employer licenses are for reading, not for ingestion.** O'Reilly bans using its content "as input or a prompt to a machine learning or AI system" ([agreement](https://www.oreilly.com/membership-agreement/), 2024-10-09). JSTOR bans LLM training, scraping and systematic downloading ([terms](https://about.jstor.org/terms/), 2026-04-24). Elsevier's website terms bar use "in combination with an artificial intelligence tool" unless a license allows it ([terms](https://www.elsevier.com/legal/elsevier-website-terms-and-conditions), 2026-03-12). Commercial text and data mining (TDM) is a separately priced product at Springer Nature and Elsevier.
- **For tool builders: link, don't ingest.** Store the catalog (identifiers, tables of contents, your notes). Send the reader to the licensed copy through their own authenticated session. Keep Claude on metadata, notes and openly licensed text unless a license explicitly covers AI processing.

## Why remote access is the hard part

- **Licenses are scoped to a population.** JSTOR says so outright. Its "Authorized Users" are walk-in users ("people allowed to access the Services while on site at an Institutional Licensee") plus listed remote users: current students, affiliated researchers and lecturers, staff, and alumni "if that Institutional Licensee has added alumni to their license" ([JSTOR terms](https://about.jstor.org/terms/), 2026-04-24). I assume other publishers' university licenses follow the same pattern. That is my reading of what the libraries publish, not of the contracts themselves [~80%]. Remote access is enforced by checking affiliation through a campus login, proxy or VPN.
- **Paid community cards don't add you to that population.** The fee buys building and borrowing privileges, which the library controls. Remote e-resources are governed by publisher contracts, which it does not. UC Berkeley says so for Wi-Fi: free visitor Wi-Fi "does not include access to Library-licensed resources" ([visitors](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visitors)). Stanford says it for all of its cards: "Access from personal devices or off campus requires a SUNet ID" ([visitor access](https://library.stanford.edu/about-stanford-libraries/visitor-access)).
- **So the routes to remote access are routes to affiliation.** At UC Berkeley the listed paths are an Extension enrollment, a visiting-scholar or postdoc appointment, retired-employee status, Extension faculty status and some campus-affiliate staff roles ([borrow & renew](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/find/borrow-renew)). Everything else is walk-in.

The same logic is closing public-library routes. LAPL restricted its e-card to Los Angeles City residents because "licensing agreements with our digital content vendors require" it ([LAPL](https://lapl.org/library-card/borrowing-policies-and-information)). See [Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/).

## UC Berkeley

### What each category gets

All rows are from the library's "Borrow & renew" page as of 2026-10-15 ([UC Berkeley Library](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/find/borrow-renew)) unless another source is linked.

| Category | Price (Oct 2026) | Remote licensed e-resources | Requirements and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visitor, no card | Free | **No** | Databases on library public computers; printing and scanning; one-day Main Stacks pass on request ([visitors](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visitors)) |
| **California resident** | **\$100/yr (\$95 seniors)** | **No** | California ID or government photo ID plus proof of California residency. 20 books; Main (Gardner) Stacks; no interlibrary borrowing |
| **Extension student** | **\$25 per 6 months** (course fee extra) | **Yes** | Proof of current registration plus photo ID. The library says "semester-length course"; Extension's help center adds "(10+ week)" |
| CSU or community-college student | \$25 per 6 months | No | Proof of current registration plus photo ID |
| Private or parochial K-12 teacher | \$100/yr | No | Government photo ID |
| UC alumni association member (California resident) | No card fee listed; association dues | No | Paid membership in one of the 10 UC alumni associations, plus proof of California residency. The card lasts as long as the membership ([alumni](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/alumni)) |
| **Visiting scholar or postdoc** | No card fee listed; appointment fee \$750 first year ([VSPA](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/about/university-services-fee)) | **Yes** | Department appointment, faculty sponsor, VSPA registration |
| Retired UC Berkeley employee; Extension faculty | No fee listed | Yes | Retiree ID or appointment |
| Stanford faculty, academic staff, postdocs, grad students | No fee listed | No | Stanford ID serves as the card. Stanford in turn gives UC Berkeley grad students, faculty and academic staff free cards ([below](#stanford)) |

**How to apply (paid cards).** Email the Privileges Desk (privdesk-library@berkeley.edu) with your contact details and documents, or go to the desk on the first floor of Doe Library. Processing takes 1–3 business days. You collect the card in person with photo ID. The desk takes cards and checks, not cash ([borrow & renew](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/find/borrow-renew)).

### Walk-in: public computers and the Gardner Stacks

"Most libraries are open to the public." Visitors without a card can do the following ([visitors](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visitors), October 2026):

- **Use the libraries' public computers** for "databases, catalogs, and educational resources". This is the free route to UC Berkeley's licensed journals. The page does not say whether you can save files to USB from those computers; I have not verified it.
- **Print and scan** in the libraries.
- **Request a one-day pass to the Main (Gardner) Stacks.** "Permission for Main Stacks access is not automatic." Longer access, up to three months, takes a separate request.

**Decision.** If what you need is articles, a walk-in session is the right first move. Buy the \$100 card only to borrow physical books. It adds no electronic access that a visitor lacks.

### The \$100 California-resident card

The \$100 card (\$95 for seniors) buys borrowing: 20 books at a time and the Gardner Stacks. It is worth buying if your work runs on print monographs that Bay Area public libraries and Link+ lack, such as older statistics, philosophy of probability or economic history.

It excludes interlibrary borrowing. For a single print-only title, Link+ through a public library is free and most requests arrive in under a week ([Public Libraries](/access/public-libraries/)). Buy the card if you expect to borrow several books a year that Link+ cannot supply [inference].

### The Extension route: a \$25 card that requires a course

This is the only route on the library's list that gives an unaffiliated person UC Berkeley's licensed e-resources from home without a sponsor. The Extension help center describes it this way (updated 2026-09-16, [Extension](https://berkeleyextension.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16655644122647-Library-use)):

- "After the start of a semester-length (10+ week) Extension course, you can purchase a \$25 6-month borrowing card."
- The card gives access to "licensed electronic resources, such as journals and databases" and up to 20 books at a time.
- You set it up at the Privileges Desk in Doe Library, or by email, with "proof of your current registration" and government photo ID.

**What the course costs.** R03 could not check course prices because Extension's catalog is rendered in JavaScript. On 2026-10-15 I queried the undocumented course web service behind the catalog pages: 20 keyword searches, 76 open sections, all online. Representative prices (the two linked rows were re-checked on their course pages):

| Course | Format | Units | Dates | Fee (Oct 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ENGLISH X135A American Fiction](https://extension.berkeley.edu/search/publicCourseSearchDetails.do?method=load&courseId=41071) | Online, Start Anytime | 3 | 90–180 days from enrollment | **\$810** |
| PSYCH X139.1 Adolescent Psychology; HISTORY XBW7A U.S. History | Online, Start Anytime | 3–4 | 90–180 days | \$910 |
| STAT X471 Introduction to Biostatistics | Online, Start Anytime | 3 | 90–180 days | \$940 |
| [COMPSCI X461 Artificial Intelligence Foundations](https://extension.berkeley.edu/search/publicCourseSearchDetails.do?method=load&courseId=86614611) | Live Online (Thursday evenings) | 2 | Oct 8 – Dec 17, 2026 | \$1,045 |
| COMPSCI X459.5 Machine Learning and Deep Learning | Online, fixed dates | 2 | Oct 13 – Dec 15, 2026 | \$1,045 |
| STAT X10 Introduction to Statistics; MATH X11 Calculus 1 | Online, Start Anytime | 4 | 90–180 days | \$1,205 |
| ECON X2 Introduction to Microeconomics | Online, Start Anytime | 3 | 90–180 days | \$1,450 |

Across the 63 sample sections worth 2 or more units, fees ran from \$665 to \$2,100, with a median of \$1,045. The cheapest, at \$665, was a 2-unit Start Anytime course, which probably fails the ten-week rule (below). The cheapest 3-unit course was \$810. The sample covers only open online sections that matched my keywords. Classroom sections were not sampled and may be priced differently.

**Two eligibility questions to settle before you pay:**

1. **Does a Start Anytime course count as "semester-length (10+ week)"?** These courses have no fixed dates. You must be enrolled "for at least 30 days per semester unit (up to 90 days)" and finish within 180 days ([Extension](https://berkeleyextension.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16681888913943-Start-Anytime-Online-Courses), updated 2026-02-05). A 3-unit course therefore runs at least 90 days, about 13 weeks; a 2-unit course's 60-day minimum falls short of ten weeks. But the minimum can be waived on request, and a self-paced course is not obviously "semester-length". I put it at [~60%] that the Privileges Desk accepts a 3-unit Start Anytime course. Ask privdesk-library@berkeley.edu, naming the course, before enrolling.
2. **Does a fixed-date course span ten weeks?** Of the 17 fixed-date fall sections in the sample, the longest ran 10 weeks from first to last date (Oct 8 – Dec 17). Most ran 9 weeks or less. A course with 10 consecutive weekly meetings spans 9 weeks on the calendar, so the date span alone does not settle it. Check with the desk.

**The arithmetic.** At the cheapest course likely to qualify, the \$810 3-unit course, one six-month window costs about \$835 (\$810 + \$25), roughly \$139 a month. Keeping access continuously means two courses a year, about \$1,670. That is more than twice the first-year visiting-scholar fee.

**The discount stack.** The Cal Alumni Association (CAA) lists "a \$50 discount per eligible UC Berkeley Extension course" among its member benefits ([CAA benefits](https://alumni.berkeley.edu/join/alumni-member-benefits/), October 2026). Its "Standard Alumni & Friends" membership is \$75/yr, and "Cal Alumni Association membership is open to all" ([CAA](https://alumni.berkeley.edu/join/)). The benefits page does not say whether the discount is limited to alumni; I put it at [~70%] that non-alumni members get it. At two courses a year the discount (\$100) only slightly exceeds the dues. Don't join for this alone.

**Don't plan on enrolling, buying the card and dropping.** Drops are refunded less a \$35 processing fee, and a Start Anytime course must be dropped within 6 days of registering ([drop policy](https://berkeleyextension.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16682930159127-Drop-a-course)). The card is sold "after the start" of a course to someone with "current registration". Neither page says what happens to the card after a drop. I assume a drop ends eligibility [~85%].

**Decision.** If you would take an Extension course anyway (statistics, ML, economics, or something unrelated you'd enjoy), the remote-access card is a \$25 add-on and the best deal in this chapter. If you would not, \$835 per six months costs more than a full visiting-scholar year and about four times a year of [JPASS](/access/subscriptions/) (\$199/yr for 120 JSTOR PDFs; [JSTOR](https://about.jstor.org/products/jpass/)), though it reaches far more publishers than JPASS. Pay it only for a bounded project, such as a six-month literature review that spans many publishers.

### Visiting-scholar appointments

A visiting-scholar appointment makes you a temporary affiliate. You get a Cal 1 Card, borrow monographs for a month at a time (up to 20 items), and reach online resources from home through links in UC Library Search or the campus VPN ([visiting scholars](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visiting-scholars), October 2026).

**What it costs** ([VSPA University Services Fee](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/about/university-services-fee), October 2026):

- Visiting scholar: **\$750** for the first year and **\$1,500** for a consecutive second year.
- Visiting student researcher: \$1,000, then \$2,500.
- "A 12-month break in between appointments reverts the reappointment fee to the 1st-year fee."
- The fee is "strictly non-prorated regardless of appointment length". Either the sponsoring department or faculty member pays, or the scholar does. If the scholar cannot, the sponsor must cover it.
- R03 notes that a department may also charge its own fee.

**Who qualifies.** Appointments must come from "a UC Berkeley department or Organized Research Unit" ([visiting scholars](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/visiting-scholars)) and are reviewed against UC policy APM-430. VSPA's exception rules show the defaults ([VSPA](https://vspa.berkeley.edu/staff-faculty/vsvsr-appointment-exceptional-request-guidelines), October 2026):

- **Degree.** A visiting scholar with only a bachelor's or master's degree needs an exception and must show "research fitness equivalent to a Ph.D., significant independent research experience, or extensive senior-level industry leadership".
- **Recent PhDs.** Someone who earned a PhD within the last five years is "typically Postdoc-eligible". An exception "is considered only if the candidate holds a professorship, a full-time professional role, or a postdoc appointment elsewhere".
- **Duration.** The standard maximum is 12 months per appointment, with a "cumulative two-year limit for Visiting Scholars". Extensions beyond two years are "not guaranteed".
- **Justification.** An exception request needs a 2–3 line research description and a 1–2 line statement of the "University Benefit".
- **Payment first.** The fee "must be paid in full before the request is submitted". The page does not say whether it is refunded if the exception is denied.

**What this means in practice** [inference, ~75%]. The route works for someone who already collaborates with a Berkeley faculty member, for example a forecasting or AI-safety researcher co-authoring with a statistics or EECS group. It is not something you can apply for cold. If you have a collaborator, \$750 buys a year of full remote access, about \$62 a month. That is the cheapest broad remote access on this page. Without a PhD, confirm the exception is likely before paying.

### Alumni

UC Berkeley gives alumni no remote licensed resources. Alumni without a card get visitor privileges, and the library points them to "freely available resources" and the Friends of the Library ([alumni](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/alumni)). "Alumni of any University of California campus who have a paid membership in any of the 10 campus alumni associations" and live in California can get a borrowing card; no card fee is stated, and it includes no remote access. CAA advertises "Get a library card at all UC campuses" as a member benefit without saying it is alumni-only, but the library's wording requires alumni status. I put it at [~70%] that a non-alumnus CAA member does not qualify.

## Stanford

Stanford sells more access tiers than Berkeley, but every one of them is on-site. "Licensed electronic resources may be accessed on designated public computers within the libraries"; off-campus or personal-device access "requires a SUNet ID" ([Stanford Libraries](https://library.stanford.edu/about-stanford-libraries/visitor-access), as of 2026-10-15). All rows below are from that page unless another source is linked.

| Category | Access only (on-site) | Access and borrowing | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Anyone: day pass** | **Free, 7 days a year** (14 for alumni) | — | Register in person at Green, Bowes Art & Architecture, East Asia or Music Library. Bring a physical government photo ID, have your photo taken, state a research purpose |
| **Independent researchers and visitors** | **\$35 / 2 weeks; \$75 / month; \$150 / 3 months; \$450 / year** | \$325 / 3 months; \$500 / 5 months; **\$1,000 / year** | Borrowing: up to 25 items, mostly 28-day loans |
| Stanford alumni | \$10 / 2 weeks; \$15 / month; \$40 / 3 months; \$100 / year | \$125 / 3 months; \$175 / 5 months; \$400 / year | Requires the SAA digital membership card, i.e. a paid SAA membership (\$795 lifetime for alumni; [SAA](https://alumni.stanford.edu/membership/)) |
| UC Berkeley grad students, faculty, academic staff | — | Free | Other UC campuses \$10. UC undergraduates and non-academic staff are not eligible |
| Short-term scholar hosted by a department | — | Free for 90 days | — |
| Stanford visiting scholar | University ID with access and borrowing | Included | Plus a SUNet ID "that allows access to certain licensed electronic resources". Fees and eligibility not checked |
| Continuing Studies students | No library privileges | — | "May be eligible for access as independent researchers" (that is, the paid cards above) |

**Excluded from all visitor cards:** the Law Library, Lane Medical Library, Hoover Library and the Graduate School of Business Library, and interlibrary loan. Card purchases cannot be prorated or refunded.

**Decisions.**

- **For e-resources, use the free day passes first.** Seven planned days a year clear a large paywalled-paper backlog [inference] (see [the session plan below](#making-a-walk-in-session-count)).
- **Buy \$35 two-week access only for a concentrated project** that needs more than seven on-site days. At four visits in two weeks it costs about \$9 a visit.
- **Stanford has no Extension-style remote route.** Continuing Studies students get no library privileges. A visiting-scholar appointment does carry a SUNet ID with some licensed e-resources, the analogue of Berkeley's appointments. Without an appointment at either university, the Bay Area's only remote option is UC Berkeley Extension.
- **Stanford alumni** need a paid SAA membership for the alumni-rate cards and the alumni database package (below). Whether the 14 free days also require membership is unclear: the library says "14 days for Stanford alumni", while SAA says "seven days (14 days for SAA members)" ([SAA perks](https://alumni.stanford.edu/perks/)).

## SF State and other walk-in options

**SF State (J. Paul Leonard Library)** is the cheapest and least bureaucratic walk-in route in San Francisco (as of 2026-10-15):

- **Public research stations.** "A limited number" on floors 1, 3 and 4 "provide on-site access to many research databases and the Library's OneSearch catalog". "No account or login is required" ([accounts](https://library.sfsu.edu/accounts)). You "can download and save information to a personal USB drive". The stations "do not provide access to email or the open web" ([community borrowers](https://library.sfsu.edu/community-borrowers)), so you cannot email files to yourself. Bring a USB drive.
- **Community Borrower card: \$50/year.** You pay by donating \$50 or more through the library's online form, then take the receipt to the Book Checkout & Pickup Desk. It allows 20 items, with 30-day loans for books and 7 days for print periodicals. It excludes "off-campus or wireless access to online databases, ebooks, online journals, and other electronic resources", interlibrary loan, and computer and printer access ([community borrowers](https://library.sfsu.edu/community-borrowers)).
- **Free special-borrower cards** go to SF State Alumni Association members, current students and faculty of other CSU campuses, and OLLI and ElderCollege members ([accounts](https://library.sfsu.edu/accounts)). The page does not say whether they include electronic access.

**Leads I could not verify** [U]:

- San José State's King Library is shared with San José Public Library, which suggests on-site database access for SJPL cardholders.
- California community-college enrollment (historically about \$46 per unit for residents; San Francisco residents may qualify for Free City College) could give student database access. CCSF and De Anza blocked automated checks, so whether part-time community-college students get remote databases is unknown. UC Berkeley's \$25 card for community-college students does *not* include remote access.

## Alumni library programs

Alumni access varies more between universities than any other route in this chapter. Check your own alma mater before paying for anything.

| Program | What you get (Oct 2026) | Cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stanford Alumni Association** | "Free access to searchable databases containing thousands of journals and publications" with SAA credentials, listed under "Exclusive Member Benefits"; alumni-rate library cards | SAA lifetime membership \$795 for alumni (\$850 in five annual payments); cards from \$10 / 2 weeks | [SAA perks](https://alumni.stanford.edu/perks/); [SAA membership](https://alumni.stanford.edu/membership/) |
| UC Berkeley alumni | No remote licensed resources; a borrowing card for UC alumni-association members in California, fee not stated | CAA Standard \$75/yr | [UCB alumni](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/help/alumni); [CAA](https://alumni.berkeley.edu/join/) |
| SF State Alumni Association members | Free special-borrower card | Association dues | [SF State](https://library.sfsu.edu/accounts) |
| JSTOR alumni access | JSTOR's terms list alumni as Authorized Users where a university "has added alumni to their license", for "the content JSTOR includes in the alumni access license". Which universities buy it was not checked | Usually free to the alumnus [U] | [JSTOR terms](https://about.jstor.org/terms/) |
| EBSCO or ProQuest "alumni editions" | Some universities license alumni database packages | Varies | R03 [U] |

**Action:** search your university's alumni site for "library", "databases" or "JSTOR". An alumni database package is remote access that no Bay Area route offers without an affiliation, a paid course or (at Stanford) association dues.
